A BRILLIANT STORY

div.head: POPULAR WRITER.
div.p: A POPULAR WRITER.
Arrangements have been made, readers will be interested to know, for the publica- tion in our columns of a story of • unusual interest entitled :
" WRITT4N IN SCARLET,*
ALICE MAUD MEADOWS.
AUTHOR OFI
"ONE LIFE BETWEEN."
"A MILLION OF MONEY."
"THE EXTREME PENALTY."
"FOR LOVE OF A LADY."
"I CHARGE YOU BOTH."

The name of MISS MEADOWS will be familiar to the most casual reader of news- paper fiction. No writer of serials is more popular throughout the country. She has a wonderful facility for the writing of sensa- tional stories, and, being one of the most industrious of literary women, has turned out an astonishing amount of work.

She was for sori.i'e years the editor of the "Princess's Novelettes," for which she wrote many of the stories herself, and was at the same time responsible for the com- panion weekly, "Something to Read," in which her own serials were running. Her output is less, but the quality of her work higher, since she put off editorial cares. Her power of holding the attention of the reader will be found exemplified, we are sure, in the story we are about to publish.
ip xyr vv R MEN IN SCARLET,"

div.head: ALICE MAD MEADOWS.
div.p: ALICE MAD MEADOWS.
OUTLINE OF PLOT.

MISS MEADOW, S writes of love and crime, and the rivalry of two brothers for a fair maiden's hand. John Brandon, a well-to-do country gentleman, is about to be married to Celia Verde. The young lady was once engaged to John's brother Dick, a wild and reckless fellow, who had gone abroad in search of adventure, and is supposed to have met his death. Celia admits that she loved the old sweetheart better than the new—in fact is doubtful whether she loves John at all. The infatuatedlover promises himself, however, that hewill win her love after marriage.

Suddenly all is changed by the return of Dick. alive and well. No one has recog- nised him except John, to whose hopes his appearance gives the death-blow. Dick laughs at the idea of Celia Verde marrying John, certain that she is true to her love for himself. The taunt excites John to fury, and in his library he re-enacts the tragedy of Cain, hiding the body in a large safe. Then a convict who has just escaped from prison appears on the scene, and, being aware of the crime, insists that Brandon shall shelter him by giving him clothes and keeping him in the house as one of the wedding guests, under the name of Vernon Salisbury.

Fresh surprises come when the safe is opened by the police, who believe the escaped convict to be concealed there, and is found empty. How this comes about Vernon Salisbury can explain, but he, too, is staggered by the disappearance of the body also from a place in the grounds where he had hidden it. Sensation, indeed, crowds upon sensation as the plot develops. The story will be followed to the end with the closest attention, the more so as to these sensational happenings is added the attractions of a strong love interest.
44 vv. VV BITTEN IN SCARLET,"
ALICE MAUL) MEADOWS.

have pained you. Ana aon-t blame me thc.:, thank Heaven with a grateful heart that no mar: lives who can snatch my great happiness from me. And in time, sweetheart, in time you shall be glad that to-morrow gives you to me. You are everything in the world to me—the heart of my heart. It is impossible I can do anlrthing but make you happy. Don't you think I shall make you happy ? " She drew from him quietly but decidedly. "How do I know ? " she answered. "1 suppose you will. I hope you will Happiness and un- happiness are, I believe, constitutional, and I am a happy person. Father once compared me to eork—nothing, he said, would keep me under. I have no fears for the future. I have no doubt but that you will make me content." He slipped his arm through hers. He did not ask agaiu for the kiss he would get it, perhaps, to-morrow. 'Co-night, evidently, was not to give it Dim. But ne understood the woman perfectly, ana ho believed, the marriage service dyer, she would be a different creature. At present she was handicapped by having been engaged twice. She had never been married. As a lover he was nothing new to her, she had had a lover before; as a husband he would be unique. They had nearly reached the house, when once more he paused. "I am like Moses," he said. "I have trampled through the wilderness, the desert; to-morrow the promised land will be all my own. Celia, sweetheart, say you are just a little glad the dear day is almost here." She shrugged her shoulders half-contempt- uously. "My life, heretofore has not. been a wilderness or a desert," she said. "We look at things from a different standpoint." "But," she grew kinder, after all she liked John very well, and it suited no purpose to make herself disagreeable. "I am glad we are to be married to-morrow. I don't think engagement time is always a happy time. I don't mean I have been unhappy—a trifle unsettled perhaps. John, I think I must go in now. I want to look my best to-morrow—a woman always does, I !oppose. There are a great many days generally in a lifetime, but, as a rule, there is not more than one wedding-day." She felt the Clasp 'of his hands tighten on her arm. ,

"Please Heaven, there shall only be one in your life," he answwed—"that we may grow old and white-haired together. Once you are all mine, really mine, I could not bear that under any circumstances you should be wife to another man, even were I dead. My spirit could not rest if--Celia, I don't think you realise how utterly I love you; it is almost terrible to worship as I do—almost an Agony ! " She laughed again. Dick Brandon, her first sweetheart, had rooked upon love less seriously, had taken the girl's affection rather as a matter of course, a right; something it was only to be expected any woman would give him did he ask for it. For this very reason, perhaps—because it had always seemed to her she might possibly lose him unless she humoured him in every way— she had given him her greatest love. With John Brandon there was no need to do more time allow herself to be worshipped. "Poor old Jack!" she said, speaking more gently. "I am afraid your love story has not been an unmitigated blessing to you. Never mind, dear, all the doubts and fears will be over to-morrow; once we are married, it's pretty certain, I think, that I shall be your very own so long as my life lasts. You are only three years older than I am, and you have three times my constitution—oh, I don't mean lam delicate; but I shall want a lot of taking care of. Now good-night "—she hesitated a minute— "good-night, sweetheart! If you stoop your head I'll kiss you, then you'll go to sleep quite, quite happy, will you not? Jack—l shall call you Jack for the future—you're trembling like a girl; you are cold." He hugged her to him as, for the very first time, she gave him a willing kiss; his whole body thrilled from head to foot, his pulses throbbed, the blood raced and rollicked in his veins.
"I love you!" he said under his breath, "Oh, Heaven, how I love you! Celia! Celia!"
CHAPTER 11.
A GHOST FROM THE PAST.

Lady Caroline Verde sat in front of her mirror, an angry look upon her pretty, well- preserved face. Three times she had touched the electric bell, that should have brought her maid to her room. Three times the summons had been unattended to. •

"That's the worst of the lower classes," the lady said to herself, "they never can take a wedding in a sensible manner. It's talk—talk— gossip—tittle-tattle! I shall be truly thankful when to-morrow is over and things settle down again. I am grateful indeed to Providence that I have only one daughter. I've had worry and trouble enough with her engagementt, and now, I suppose, I'm to wait my maid's pleasure, because she must talk things over. I particu- larly wished to get to bed early, I most ardently hope the papers will say something pretty about my looks—that it seemed impossible I could be the young bride's mother—l've been a widow three years, the situation is growing monotonous. I've half a mind to put myself to bed."
She touched the electric bell/ again, keeping her finger on it for some timer; then suddenly the door of her bedroom opened, and her maid entered.

She was dressed for walking, her face was very pale, her eyes looked frightened. She shut the door, and dropped into a chair. Lady Caroline looked at her with displeasure and surprise. "Well, I'm sure!" she said. "What do you mean by keeping me waiting? And how dare you sit down in my presence? I particularly wished to get to bed early—l distinctly told you so. I'm sure I 'don't know what servants are coming to. Go and take your hat off immediately, and come back to me." The girl did not move. "Oh, my lady!" she said. "Oh, my lady! how can I tell you? Oh, I thought I should have died! Back from the dead, after more than a year! Oh, my lady! what will happen ? What will Miss Celia say ? " It was evident that for some reason or other the girl was on the verge of hysterics. Lady Caroline rose, went to her, and shook her soundly...

"Wliat's the matter?" she asked. "What has happened? What in the world do you mean about Miss Celia? If I didn't know whatever your other faults may be that you are a teetchler, I should think you'd been drinking. Pu,l yourself together, and don't be a fool !" Another vigorous shake, perhaps, helped the girl to overcome some fear or emotion. She took her handkerchief from her pocket and wiped her damp brow; she tottered to her feet for an instant, but sank back again on to the chair. Lady Caroline hesitated an instant, then mixed her some sal volatile.

"Drink that," she said, "and tell me what is the matter. Really,it's most inconsiderate of you, when I so much wished to look well to-morrow. I shall simply be a wreck. I can't—l never could—stand worry. How can you be so incon- siderate?" She administered another shake; the repetition of the dose completely pulled the girl together. "Oh. my lady, it was awful!" she said. "Horrible! I was walking quite alone— it wouldn't have been so horrible if I'd had anyone with me—l was _passing through the wood, on the footpath; it Inds straight, as you know, to Mr. John Brandon's house; I was thinking about the wedding, but I'm sure I was not thinking of Mr. Dick, only of Miss Celia and Mr. John. And then, all at once, I heard step ii behind me, quick, long steps, and a man whistling." She paused, looking round in a frightened way. Lady Caroline sat down. "Well, well, what of that ? " she said. “Gol, on, girl. Good Heavens! Do you think I've nothing to do but listen to your rigmaroles ? I i tell you I'm tired—dead beat. What does it matter if a man did whistle as he came through , the wood—it didn't kill you, did it ? " 1 "Oh, my lady!" the girl answered, "don't you remember how he used to whistle wherever he went—whistle, whistle ? It flashed through me oven before I turned. I thought to myself, that's just like Mr. Dick, just his way, just the songs he used to whistle—the gay, reckless songs. And then I turned, and there he was' Oh, my laity, I thought I should have died! Back from the grave—on the. eve of poor Miss Cel is.' s wedding-day ! " Lady Caroline turned pale; she was startled, but she did not in the least take in what the girl meant. "He? Who P" she asked. "Have you gone crazy ? " The girl shivered. "That's just what thought,' she answered. "Have I gone crazy_ am I stark, staring mad! There we were looking at one another; me in the flesh, him in the snirit—come back from the crave. because he

minion s rest wan Miss Celia going to give herself to another. Oh, my lady! there he was, just the same as ever—just as handsome, just as smiling—poor, perturbed spirit that he is! Just as reckless as we all knew him. I looked and looked, never speaking; then A gave one great scream and tore for my life, thinking he was after me all the time. Oh, my lady J what does it mean ?" _ _ _ _

The girl was so evidently scared that Lady Caroline grew frightened also; more seriously, though less emotionally, alarmed than the girl. She was a level-headed woman, and did not believe in ghosts. Was it possible, after all, that Dick Brandonlihad not died? That he had come back, at the most unfortunate time possible? Personally, she had never been con- vinced of his death, and had wondered at Celia believing in it so quickly. It had seemed to her he was not the sort of man to allow adverse fate - to wipe him out so easily. However, John Brandon had been much more satisfactory from the son-in-law point of view than his younger brother; better off, for one _ thing, very much more steady, less likely to give his wife or his wife's mother trouble. Lady Caroline had liked Dick, it was almost impossi- ble not to do so; but she had not been sorry when the rumour of his death came, and Celia. accepted the news as true. Lady Caroline rose from her seat, and crossing the room, locked the door. The last person she \ wanted to come to her now was her daughter. Then she came back to the girl, and laid her hand on her shoulder. "You have imagined this, of course," she said. "You have let your ridiculous fancies run riot; but even a fancy may do a lot of harm. Whom else . _

have you mentionedthis absurd nonsense to 2 The girl was still too scared even to look hurt. "To no one, my lady," she answered. "I came straight to you; but it's no nonsense, no imagination. I saw him as plain as plain—just as he was in the flesh. In another minute I believe he would have spoken to me; if he had. I should have died! Oh, my lady! do you think Miss Celia ought to know? To think the poor young man can't rest because she's giving herself to another—it's horrible horrible! it's bad enough to keep a human being in torture, one who can fight for himself.; but a spirit—oh, it seems heartless and cruel! I came to you first, but I think Miss Celia ought to know." Lady Caroline's lips set in a very hard lino. Most of her friends looked upon her as a pretty, x•ft, romantic little creature; she looked hard as jails now. "You've a good place here," she said, "and you're not so _stnnid thnt you el,..>+ •

you•ve more liberty Gnan one girl out of hundred; you've the menservants to flirt and coquette with; you're just about as comfortably placed as a girl in your position can be. You've suited me very well so far, and I've no wish to part with you; but breathe a word of this to Miss Celia, and out you go, neck and crop. You've been thinking of Mr. Dick, and you've imagined the whole affair, but quite understand this—l won't have Miss Celia unsettled. Mr. Dick was never satisfactory; Mr. John i eminently so. If you've quite recovered yourself I shall bo glad if you 'II take down my hair, and next time you feel hysterical, be good enough to postpone the attack until I have done with your services for the day. I don't in the least mind your imagining ghosts .or spirits, or being upset, so long as you don't obtrude your bothers on me. You've eaten something that has disagreed with you. I hope you'll be able to remember what, I so that it may not occur again."
CHAPTER 111. EACH FROM THE DE.

Figuratively speaking, John Brandon walked noon air as he left his sweetheart. She had kissed him! Every lover knows that is some- Thing very different from one's sweetheart just allowing herself to be kissed. Thinking it over, it seemed to him she had kissed him quite fondly, almost passionately. Woman, he knew, is a complex creature. Was it possible, after all, that she loved him? There was no reason why she should not; other women had been willing enough to do sO, and since love begets love there was. every reason why she should. Second love, like second thoughts, is sometimes best. Her teasing, seeming indifference, might only have mk for a. a•raa* off e.n4 nr
Anyway, she had kissed him—to live until the morning that was quite sufficient- . . .

There is always something pathetic about a great passion. A true, deep love ever verges on the tragic; the higher we Climb, the deeper may we fall. John Brandon IVA just on top notes as he Walked homewards; very . much disturbed, very much excited—almost perfectly happy. "Celia is a good, true woman," he said to himself, "and good, women always love their husbands—that is natural; one See it throughout creation. Celia, whatever her feelings are now, will love me. And there can be no doubt—none what- ever—but that I shall make her happy; far, far happier than Dick—poor Dick !—could have done. He was not built for matrimony: his affections 9wld never have remained fixed for long upon one A nrizs once gained became valueloo` to him, 1 have seen tnat again Ana again, whereas my treasures grow dearer to me day by day—and my wife will be the greatest treasure of them all ! "

He walked slowly, enjoying the cool breeze, the damp mist of a somewhat inclement evening, the darkness that seemed to wrap him round in a cloak of moisture. Inwardly he was so happy, so joyous, he was almost glad the night was what some would have called disagreeable, because of the contrast; ,nothing, he told himself, could have depressed him. He looked upward at the dark sky, and laughed. "It will rain to-night—let it come down!" he said aloud. " ' Howl winds, crack your cheeks —howl, rage.' What a fool I am—what a happy, happy, lucky fool!" A moment ago there had been almost utter silence; now behind him he heard the crisp, fallen twigs cracking under the footsteps of some- one who followed him.

"No one so lucky as I," he said to himself; "no one whose heart is so crowded with pure joy. Someone with a light, quick step—lighter and quicker than mine, but no one with such an utter joy nestling in his bosom!" The steps were close behind him; the man, whoever he was, almost swung by him, turning his head as he did so. The light that pierced the trees was dim, but something in the whole figure was familiar, horribly familiar. John Brandon's heart, beat loudly, a sense of sickness over- whelmed him.

The man paused, peered Into his face, then with a laugh clapped him on the shoulder. "Jack, old man !" he said, heartily, "Jack, I've come back. I saw a familiar face once before to-night, and the girl ran screaming away. I understoo? -•

lie Tookea rouna, the wood was very dark, wry lonely. A temptation—a supreme temptation.-- came to him, dominated him absolutely for a minute; then, as it were, he got the beast by the throat, grappled with, throttled it. Whatever happened, it must not be murder—the brand of Cain—but how else?

to him a sort of paralysis had fallen upon With an effort he moved his lips. "You have startled me," he said. "I thought— you know what I thought—what we all have thought—that you were dead. We had better go home, had we not? We can talk there." His voice was steady, his tone cold. The younger mAn shrugged his shoulders. "You're not exactly enthusiastic," he said; "you haven't even said you're pleased to see me! By all means, let us go home; but first answer this question—Celia is quite well ? " "Quite well," John returned, but his voice sounded strangely harsh, "Unmarried, of course ?* John Brandon looked at his brother; through the half.blackness of a dark night his eyes blazed. Could Dick have seen his face properly he would have thought the expression anything but pltasant. "Unmarried—yes," he returned.
He mentioned' nothing of the wedding bells which were to ring on the morrow. That they should ring he was determined; no man should cheat him of his happiness now—it was ton near, too dear to him."

"Nothing shall keep her from me!" he said to himself. And the wind, careering through the black, dark trees, seemed to whisper that to reach his happiness there was only one way. Celia did not hoe him; Celia still loved this man, who walked strong and stalwart by his side. If she had to choose between them it would not be he, John, whom she would lhoose. "She shall not choose!" he said to himself. 'There are two men in Streatley who love her now—by, to-morrow I will have whittled them lown to one!" But how? _ _

div.head: WRITTEN IN SCARLET.
div.p: WRITTEN IN SCARLET.
By ALICE MAUD MEADOWS, Author of "One Life Between," "A Million of Money," "The Extreme Penalty," "For Love of a Lady," "I Charge You Both," &e.

div.head: CHAPTER I.
div.p: CHAPTER I.
THE WEDDING EVE.

It was the wedding eve of Celia Verde and John Brandon. A short engagement—short because the min was adoring and impatient, thel woman indifferent to everything—on the morrow would culminate in matrimony. It was eleven o'clock. Celia, with a trifle more consideration than was usual for her lover, had walked with him to the garden gate. There they were saying their good-bye, passionately loving on the man's part; for once, just a trifle nervously on the woman's. There is probably no hour more full of romance and emotion in the life of a man and woman than the hour in which for the last time they take leave of one another as lovers, to meet on the following day at Cis to be bound together, for better for wo. . .11 the Holy Bond of wedlock. Love may, or may not, burn in both hearts; that, however, makes little difference to the intensity of the situation. One life is, as it were, , closints., the page is almost turned down; the book oi an absolutely new existence lies ready to open when the wedding bells chime out. Heart, body, and soul, John Brandon loved, had loved all his manhood's years, the girl who to-morrow was to be his wife. For twelve long months she had once been engaged to his brother —while John ate his heart out with gnawing jealousy—a wild, adventurous spendthrift, who had ultimately gone abroad to make his fortune, and, so report said, died in West Africa. While his brother lived John Brandon had kept his love locked within his heart, though many had guessed at it.. A man may bite his tongue, may lock back words with clenched teeth, compressed lips, but the eyes own no master, obey no orders; and John Brandon's eyes betrayed his secret. With his brother's death he felt he had a right to woo the woman he loved, and lips became as communicative as his eyes had been. Why Celia Verde accepted John Brandon she could not have told; perhaps because, as she assured herself—there are women who really be- lieve they must marry someone—she must marry. She did not love him in the least, but she liked him. He never touched her heart, but sometimes she could not deny to herself his passionate wooing—different, more intense than that of the spendthrift ne'er-do-well lover—stirred her deeper feelings somewhat. Anyway, love and love's blandishments were not unpleasant to her. She felt she would be happier married than single—in fact, the idea of the life of an old maid was more than distasteful to her—and probably she would. It was a dark, blustering night. The heavens -were black so black and starless it was impossible it, see whether rain clouds hung low down towards the earth; the air was damp. • John Brandon's arm was round Celia. He .pulled a fleecy wrap she wore more closely about her. "I shall take you back," he said. "It's too good of you to come with me, but not a fit night for you to be out. There's a dampness in the air, and I wouldn't have you catch cold for a fortune. Give me one kiss, Celia. I don't think you have ever kissed me." He brought her to a standstill, put his arms round her, drew her close to his heart. She could feel its quick pulse, its rise and fall, and laughed softly. Somehow, the love of John always amused her, though it interested her too. To her he was more a subject than a lover. She liked to analyse, almost to vivisect his feel- ings and emotions. He was, perhaps, as much in her life as he would have been had she loved him—as, of course, she would in time. Wives always do; the very rare exceptions only prove the rule. "Never kissed you?" she repeated. "I have kissed you a hundred times, or you me." "A very different thing. A man who loves a woman craves for something more than a passive sweetheart. Celia, I want to ask you a question. Will you answer it?" She could not, see his face, but she could feel that he trembled. She almost knew what the question would be. "I suppose so," she answered. "Yes, of • course I shall answer it. Why should I not? I hope it is nothing disagreeable." He let her go a little, not releasing her entirely, yet not keeping her so closely a prisoner. "I hope not," he said. "Celia, you remember my brother ? " He felt her form stiffen. Her voice, when she answered, was hard and cold. "Of course I remember him. It would be rather strange, would it not, if I had forgotten him?" He pushed his hat back from his brow; the cool night wind fanned him comfortingly. "I suppose it would; and yet I could wish you had forgotten him. I am jealous of him now sometimes, though he is dead—though he is out of your life. You loved him. I don't know whether you—" He broke off, remained silent for a minute, then once more his clasp grew close and strong. "He is dead—dead!" he said. "And since I love you that is a good thing in my eyes, though he was my brother, though I cared for him. To-morrow you are to be my wife. After to-morrow, nothing but death will have power to part you from me. But suppose—it is a ridiculous idea—but suppose you still had us two to choose between, which would you choose? My love for you in comparison with his is as wine to water. What about yours?" She looked up. He could see her shining eyes in the more than semi-darkness, her white face. "I have never pretended to love you," she said, slowly. "You said it was enough if I would let you love me—that in time, after our marriage, my love would come. Anyway, that you would make me happy, and so I let you love me. With the other it was different." "Ydu loved him ? " "Yes." "You have not forgotten him?" "No. I never stall forget him. Perhaps—l don't know—l marry his brother because it seems to me by so doing I shall creep a little closer to him. Why do you ask such questions? It can't be pleasant to receive such answers." • "And if "—the man's tone and face were hard— "he could come back from the dead, there would be no chance for me?" "None—oh, none!" "You would throw me aside like a worn-out glove ? " "I should be true to my original promise. Take me in, I am cold." He bent his lips to hers; she could feel his breath hot on her cheek. "Kiss me find." he said, "and forffivn i?

div.head: SCIENCE ,NOTES AND NEWS.
div.p: SCIENCE ,NOTES AND NEWS.
FIREPROOF CELLULOID.

A process has been invented for rendering cel- luloid non-inflammable. In its broad principles the prcicess may be said to consist of introducing into the mass of celluloid, when it has reached the highest degree of, fluidity during its manu- facture, a certain quantity of a salt, such as phosphate, bicarbonate oi ammonia, or magnes- ium, or still others. These salts possess the pro- perty of giving off under the influence of heat a great quantity of gas, which stops the progress of the combustion. It is claimed that quantities of uninflammable celluloid can be manufactured by the new process into any form and size desired.

div.head: FAUNA OF LAKE TANGANYIKA.
div.p: THE FAUNA OF LAKE TANGANYIKA.

The view that the unique fauna of Lake Tan- anyika indicates a former connection of this sheet of water with tho ocean does not receive confirmation from Calman's recent paper in the "Proceedings of the Zoological Society." The shrimps which he describes from the great Afri- can lake are of an essentially fresh-water type, and do not show any close affinities with marine forms. Tanganyika, however, possesses a large number of species peculiar to itself, and not found in adjacent lakes. Along with the rest of the fauna they are considered to be the result of long-continued divergent evolution, and speciali esti= due to isolation.

div.head: lODINE BLUE.
div.p: lODINE BLUE.

The blue colour produced by the action si iodine on starch is so familiar to all students of elementary chemistry that it is somewhat surprising to learn that the exact nature oi the phenomenon has not yet been determined by chemists. According to Kiisten it is not a definito chemical compound, but a result of the absorption of the iodine by the starch. Messrs. Padosa and Savare, however, attacking the pro- blem in a different way, ' have come to a some- what different conclusion. Adding some starch to a solution of iodine in potassium iodide, they investigated the resulting changes in the electri- cal conductivity of the liquid. They conclude from their observations that the blue substance is a compound of starch, potassium iodide, and iodine, the iodine and starch being in the ratio of one to four.

div.head: TOWARDS THE ABSOLUTE ZERO.
div.p: TOWARDS THE ABSOLUTE ZERO.

Various considerations have led physicists to fix upon 273 deg. below zero on the Centigrade thermometer as absolute zero, the absence of all heat. This means 491 deg. below freezing-point on the more familiar Fahrenheit. Recent re- searches with liquid air and liquid hydrogen are leading physicists nearer And nearer to this nadir of temperature. Thus, Professor Dewar has been able to record an absolute temperature of 13deg. that is 13deg. above absolute zero, or 260 deg. below zero Centigrade. Is there any prospect of a still lower temperature being at- tained? Helium has not yet been liquified, hav- ing resisted all the devices by which even such refractory gases as nitrogen and hydrogen have been reduced. The inferencii, the Globe thinks, is that helium has a lower boiling-point than hydrogen. Hence, if it ever is reduced, then liquid helium will furnish us with an even lower temperature than the lowest yet registered by means of liquid hydrogen.
MALLEABLE IRON DIRECT FROM ORE.

A new process for directly converting iron ore into malleable iron or steel by a continuous sys- tem has been made by two Australians, Messrs. Heskett and Moore. It is claimed that the new discovery will effect a saving of 25 per cent. in the manufacture. The ore is simply concentrated by ordinary methods, or, if it is magnetic, it is separated electrically until the pure oxide of iron is obtained. The oxide of iron is passed through a revolving cylinder heated by waste gases from subsequent operations, and brought in that cylin- der to a dull red heat. It drops from the cylin- der to a second similar cylinder, and in the latter it is brought into contact with the deoxidising gas, which is forced through and brought into contact with the heated ore. The heated ore is thus converted into a pure iron. Accompanied by and protected by the deoxidising. gas, it is passed into a third chamber or melting hearth, where it falls into a bath of molten iron, and Is converted directly into steel or balled up as mal- leable iron.

div.head: WIND POWER AND ELECTRICITY.
div.p: WIND POWER AND ELECTRICITY.

The Engineering News gives particulars of whas is stated to ho a successful utilisation of wind in the generation of electrical energy. The plant, which is installed at Noblesville, Indiana, appears to be of a somewhat complicated de- scription, and consists in part of a 14ft. wind- mill on a 50ft. tower. This drives a plunger pump which delivers water to a reservoir in which a constant pressure of 751 b. per square inch is maintained, by weights mounted on a plunger in the reservoir. This water, under pressure, is used when necessary to drive a h.p. turbine wheel which is direct-connected to a 0.-p. 25-volt dynamo, for charging the storage battery. The battery' consists of eleven cells, arid lights twenty Bc.-p. lamps for three hours or Eve 80.-p. lamps for six hours. Ordinarily, the windmill should run five hours per day to gene- rate sufficient current for winter use, and two hours per day for summer use. Automatic hydraulic devices, however, enable the pump to store any amount of energy the windmill may produce. • SUGGESTIONS FOR THE DEAF.

In the ,•apartment of Mrs. A. M. Town, of Utica, New York, is an arrangement of electrical lights that is of practical service to those who cannot hear the ringing of the " door-bell and telephone-bell. When the telephone-bell rings in the rear of the apartment, a brilliant light flashes up in the front-room, and remains lighted until turned Off. This light is so arranged that it flashes into the looking-glasses of three rooms. A light can be placed in every room if desired. , The electric door-bell is arranged in a similar way, the light being of another colour. The ar- rangement has, according to the Scientific Am erican, proved satisfactory and inexpensive. Most deaf people can hear over a telephone. By adopting this plan, a telephone is quite as useful to a deaf person as to one who can hear. In case of illness, when the ringing of bells is to be avoided, this arrangement seems an admirable one. When the lights are used, the bell is also retained. A movable bulb that can be taken to any part of the house is a great convenience. , The door-bell in that case is silent.

div.head: WITCHES' BROOMS.
div.p: WITCHES' BROOMS.

Witches' Brooms are of frequent occurrence where birch trees are found, and are seen most frequently on these trees. They consist of densely-massed clusters of small twigs, and look something like birds' nests in the ' branches. They are considered to be of the nature of galls, and to be caused by the growth, in the tree of species of fungi. The exact method of forma- tion, however, seems a little obscure and uncer- tain. Witches' Brooms may occur also on other trees, as the pear tree, and in a German scien- tific journal Emil Heinricher describes some ex- periments with these growths as occurring on the cherry tree. He finds, for example, that by grafting a twig from the broom on to another tree this latter is infected with the disease, and becomes a broom-bearer. Heinricher also finds that spontaneous infection by the transference of the fungus spores from one tree to another is of rare occurrence. The fungus causing the growth of the brooms of the cherry is a species of Exoascus. It is another species of Exoascus which produces the curl disease in the almond tree, causing the leaves to crumple up in 8, curi- ous way, and assume a brilliant scarlet colour.

div.head: SHAPE OF THE SUN.
div.p: THE SHAPE OF THE SUN.

That there is a variation in the figure of the sun has long been suspected. Observations ap- parently confirming this variation have been published by Ambronn •sinbodying • heliomete: measures made with the Gottingen heliometer during 1890-1902. Schur determined a series of measures of the solar diameter throughout the whole of a sun-spot cycle of eleven years or thereabout, and, to obviaeo errors as far as pos- sible, two complete and independent series of ob- servations were made by himself and Ambronn. In their discussion Ambronn found the mean solar diameter for the . whole series; then the residual for each observation by subtracting the mean. From these residuals ho obtained the mean residual for each year, and thus the yearly variation in diameter. The table of these varia- tions shews a periodicity with a time of between six and eight years. C. L. Poor, in ,an article appearing in the Astrophysical Journal, considers that this method could not lead 'to the detection of any changes in the diameters, and rediscusses the whole series 4 values. Ho detects a decided periodicity, the,' polar diameter Wing larger in 1890-1, while the equatorial diameter was greatest during 1892, 1393, and 1894. The exact length of the period is uncertain, but it appears to be nearly, the 'same as the sun-spot period. The amplitude of the variation is o.2sec., the dif- ference between the largest positive and nega- tive values beim g about O'Ssee. These heliometer measures thus corrohorate the conclusions pre- viously determined from Rutherford's photo- graphs, but the amplitude of the variation Is much less in the case of the visual observation*.

Red, Rough, Raw, or Cracked Skin Soothed and Healed by Zam-Buk.

div.head: HOUSE OF LORDS. Junior Liberals in Debate.
div.p: THE HOUSE OF LORDS. Junior Liberals in Debate.
AMP

It was due to the Junior Liberal Association that the members of the Progressive Labour League should have mustered in greater force for the debate on Monday evening, on the House of Lords. As it was their ranks were but thinly represented, with the result that the Junior Liberals had no serious opposition to face, and carried all before them, Mr. George Walker presided. The proceedings were opened by Mr. JOSEPIL HAwTHORN, who moved :—" That this House, while recognizing the necessity for a Second Chamber in the constitution of this country, considers that such Second Chamber should be representative and not hereditary." —Mr. Hawthorn lost no time in introducing his subject, but at once proceeded to vigorously condemn the con- duct of the hereditary Chamber. "We are met " he said "at p time when we have a vivid example of how the House of Lords applies the brake to the Liberal Legislation in the treatment of the Education Bill. In their wildest flights of imagination the Lords could not point to the Bishops Bill' of 1902 as being a real expression of the will of the 'people but nevertheless the Bishops were allowed to hay their way. Immediately the Liberal Government assumes office and seeks to remove some of the grievances imposed upon Nonconformists— grievances admitted by the most zealous cleric—the Lords begin to talk of their constitutional right to prevent hasty and foolish legislation." Proceeding he said he was not going to give a long catalogue of the misdeeds of the Lords.A record had recently been given them of the votea of the Bishops in the House of Lords during the 19th century and sorry reading it was to a. thoughtful Christian. It had been shown that the Bishops had used their power primarily for the protec- tion of the interests of the Established Church. Their' idea of advancing religious welfare was to vote steadily for the exclusion of all other denominations from the elementary rights of citizenship while on' the Education Question their attitude had been one of steady opposition to popular control. Liberal measures for the enfranchisement of the people were tabooed factory legislation had a frigid recbption and never once had the Bench of Bishops thrown its weight into the scale of peace when the balance trembled. If that much was to be 'said of the Lords spiritual what was to be said of the destructive work of the Lords temporal ? In the words of Mr. Chamberlain " the chronicles of the House of Lords are one record of concessions delayed until they have lost their grace, of rights denied until extracted from their fears. It has been a history of one long contest between the representatives of privilege and the representatives of popular rights, and during that time the Lords have perverted, delayed and denied justice until at last they gave, grudgingly and churlishly, what they could no longer withhold." They did not wish to place rough hands on what was a picturesque institution by reason of its long connection with the history of the cour.try, but it was time for them to insist upon the governMent of the people, by the people and for the people. div.head: FOR THROAT AND LUNGS.
div.p: FOR THROAT AND LUNGS.
How Peps Cure that Nasty Cough.

MAYOR AT CHURCH.

His Worship the Mayor (Alderman Samuel Owens) attended Divine service at the Primitive Methodist Chapel, Frederick-street, Widnes, in state on Sunday morning. At a quarter past ten the pasession left the Town Hall in the following order :—Artillery Engineers and Volunteers, the Mayor, ex-Mavor, Town Clerk, and Alderman W. W. Gossage, COuncillors, Gossage's Prize Band, officials of the Town Hall, fire brigade.and representatives of the various public bodies The service in chapel was conducted by the Rev' G. S. Delalield.who gave an eloquent discourse on the st.l,ject Of " Citizenship." The collection taken was in aid of the Nurses' Fund. The procession wended its way back to the Town Hall, aniwas witnessed by large crowds of people who thronged the streets.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The Queen's Christmas Cards.—lf Christmas 'cards go out of favour it will not be for want of enterprise on the part of their producers. It seems early yet to be thinking of Yule-tide, except we have friends to send to in far distant lands, but in making a few purchases for these, one is struck by the fact that in beauty of design and artistic charm, the Christmas cards this season surpass those of all previous years. The Queen always has her Christmas cards specially prepared, 'early in the season, and on this occasion it is taken from a picture in her Majesty's possession, of a familiar 'Yule-tide scene in Denmark. It represents a little snow covered country cottage to the eaves of which the occupants are engaged in tying up a bundle of hay, in order that the birds may find warmth and comfort during the festive season. The card with appropriate Words of greeting is beautifully got up, enclosed in delicate cream folders, and strapped with helitrope ribbon. The Princess Royal.—The Duchess of Fife has -unhappily not altogether recovered from the effects of her recent severe illness, and it is possible that Her Royal Highness will go abroad this winter. It would be quite contrary to custom for the Duke and Duchess have invariably spent the winter at Brighton,where they lead a very quiet and domestic life, and go little into Society. The Riviera has never had any attractions for their, but it is probable that the Duchess will go to the Mediterranean this winter, unless her health consider- ably improves. Her two daughters have almost arrived at an age when travelling would be consideed a neces- sary part of their education, and this too may have its effect upon the disinclination which the Princess Royal has always had to living abroad. The King of Roumania.—lt is said that King Charles of Roumania is suffering from the same incurable disease as caused the death of the Emperor of Russia, and also that his illness is an advanced stage of its course, He IS in his sixty-seventh year, and was an Hohenzollern prince when he accepted the crown of Roumania forty Tears ago. He married about the same time the charm- ing Princess Elizabeth of Wied, now Queen Elizabeth, the brilliant author, painter, musician, and. poet, who is known throughout the world as "Carmen Sylva." King Charles' heir is the nephew Prince Ferdinand who married Princess Marie, eldest daughter of our then Duke of Edinburgh. The Kaiser and his Cousin—The German Emperor has not been worried so often as the Emperor of Austria .over a family mesalliance, but he appears to have had some trouble with his cousin Prince Joachim Albrecht, who has long been a conspicuous personage in Berlin's gayest social circle. The Prince is the central figure of a story, according to which he wanted to marry an Austrian actress. One obstacle to the wedding was tha react that the lady was not "noble," so a marriage of took etteenec e was arranged with a real Baron, which that d' at a London registry office,it being intimated tvorce should Prince e free immediately follow, when the would be ; to marry the Baronness. There ' appears to have been some squabbling over the com- mission to be paid when it was all carried through, and the whole thing becoming a Court Scandal, the Kaiser hi. as stepped in to nip it in the bud, by ordering Prince oachim and his regiment on foreign service, on the West Ceast of Africa, which seems a little hard on his brotimr officers and men. A Great Parti.—An alliance with one of the daughters of the Duke and Duke and Duchess of Rutland is rumoured for Lord Anglesey, who is one of the most important and wealthiest of the young unmarried peers. He and his mother, the widowed Lady Alexander Paget, have been entertaining a good deal at Warwick House in London, during the season, and at Plas Newydd, in Anglesey, wherelhe Duchess of Rutland and two of her daughters have been staying. There seemed at one time little prospect of Lord Anglesey succeding to the Marquisate, as he was only a cousin of the late eccentric peer, but having done so, he has become a very eligible parti, and is expected to make a brilliant marriage, as did his two sisters, Lady Ingestre and Lady Herbert. A Famous Pack of Hounds.—The Duke of Rutland's hounds at Belvoir, which have commenced their Leicestershire season, owns a pedigree dating back to 1750, about the time when fox-hunting first began to be a fashionable pursuit of Society. They were one of the first packs to be established "solely to fox," and the kennel books at Belvoir, of which the late uke of Rutland was very proud, have been carefully kept since 1750. Prior to that foxes were hunted, but mainly only With a view to compassing their death by any of the readiest means possible. There are now over 300 packs of foxhounds at work in Britain alone, one of which is the newly-started pack, the Northumberland Hounds, founded by Mrs. Nancy Burrell of Carham Sensible Modes.—lt is a matter of common remark, how much happier the woman out for a constitutional, and on a shoppingtour looks nowadays, to what she did, under similar circumstances, in times gone by. And When we come to consider the matter, there appears Very good reason why we should look happier. First Find foremost we are permitted, a. really short skirt, • \Mich relieves us from all anxiety with regard to ,fitreeping the roads and pavements, moreover both 'lands are free. Then again boots and shoes a size too Small, are not fashionable. The woman who a decade Or two back really took a " four," but preferred to endure the torture of a " three," is no longer in evidence. If we need a "five" we take it, and it appears that a " six " is not infrequently in demand •among smart Society women. Then we have given up high heels, a low heeled boot or shoe, with a sensible Sole being the favourite footgear with the woman who Walks. Again great improvements have been made in Our rain coats and mackintoshes, from the useful as well as the ornamental point of view, and these garments which by the way rarely exceed three quarter length in no wnv now impede the weaver's progress. And there is little prospect, in these days when out door exercise and recreations have, gained so firm a hold upon our affections that we shall again allow Dame Fashion to hamper U 3 as she did—so disastrously, and overwhelm- ingly—in days gone by. Chiffon Velveteen.—The appearance of chiffon velveteen will be hailed with delight by all those women who have found the lovely chiffon velours we have bad with us for several seasons now, beyond their purse. The new fabric is a delightful one, in every sense of the word; it falls, and drapes most artistically, and promises to wear well. Bands of silk piped with velveteen form the trimming on many of the newly built chiffon velveteen gowns, but opinions are divided as to whether cloth is not a more modish and effective OrnamOOtatiOn. Muff Chains.—The assortment of muff chains is almost bewildering, and this form of Christmas and New Year gift, seems likely to prove a popular one. The woman however who does not possiss a muff chain can easily manufacture one for herself. First she will need some narrow moire ribbon of the same shade as the Inuff,and this she should sew over with paillettes,or beads of a little lighter or darker hue. Numberless bowls of curious and paillettes are to be found on the •counters of all the big drapery houses, and a novel- looking, and very inexpensive muff chain is not a difficult item to manufacture. Mrs. Gaskell's Works.—Six out of the eight volumes contained in Messrs. Smith,Elder,and Co.'s new edition of Mrs. Gaskell's works—the " Knutsford Edition " are now published, " Sylvia's Lovers " baying appeared oarly in the week. "Cousin Phyllis" due lob November '26 and "Wives and Daughters" on December 10. This Charming edition is one the many lovers of Mrs. Oaskell's ks will greatly admire and. appreciate. MAD GE.

div.head: MEXICAN RUBBER.
div.p: MEXICAN RUBBER.

The directors of Chilian Exploration and Development , Syndicate, Limited, have received a cablegram from the chairman of the Syndicate (Mr. C. S. Treacher) in full agreement with the director of the Syndicate (Mr. P. Jefferson Brewer) who accompanied Mr. Treacher on his mission to Mexico. These gentlemen have safely reached the Syndicate's Freehold Land Estates of 20,000 acres in the famous State of Oaxaca, the garden spot of Mexico. The late storms in Mexico did not touch the Syndicate's Estates. Of immense importance to the Syndicate is the fact that Mr. Trencher has made most careful experimental tappings of the rubber trees on the Syndicate's plantations, and has unquestionably proved the fact that the 24,000 mature rubber trees are the true " Castilloa Elastica," the rubber trees which Sir Daniel Morris, K.C.M.G., &c., so strongly recommends above all others for cultivation and investment. The circum- ferance of the Castilloa Elastica trees measured by Mr. Treacher and Mr. Brewer, on the Syndicate's plantations (the trees being taken casually) was 3ft. to 71t. Dr. Aguirre the Syndicate's legal representative in,. Vern- Cruz. Mexico 'has thoroughly examined the Title a to the 20,000 acres of freehold land, the property of the Syndicate, and the Syndicate has just received a certifi- cate from him that the titles are all in order and free from any encumbrances of any kind whatsoever.

div.head: UNABLE TO EAT.
div.p: UNABLE TO EAT.
Dundee Lady tells of Loss of Appetite, followed by Pain, Wind, Headache, and Dizziness. _

I had dreadful head- sales, and was a perfect martyr to wind, with frequent dizzy attacks ; and sometimes I went off in a dead faint. div.head: PADGATE.
div.p: PADGATE.

ALE OF WORK AT PADGATE.—A sale of icork in aid of Dr. Stephenson's Orphanage, wits held in Padgate Wesleyan Schools on Saturday afternoon. There was a large attendance at the opening ceremony which was performed by Mrs. Withinshaw.—Mrs. Harris, who pre- sided, said she thought the sympathy of all was with the object in view. (Applause).—Mrs. Within- shaw, who was received with applause, said she had great sympathy with the work in which they were engaged in the Young Leaguers' Union, as hq heart always went out to little children. She vasfpleased they were trying to help them, as it would no doubt enable them to live happier and nobler .lives. She had much pleasure in declaring the sale open. (Applause.) —A hearty vote of thanks was passe a to Mrs. Harris for presiding and to Mrs. Withinshaw for opening the sale. —Concerts were given at intervals and thoroughly enjoyed. The artistes were Miss Mabel Henshall, Mr. W. Clay, Mr. J. Clayton, Mr. Ambrose St. John (humorist), of Manchester. and Mrs. Forman (pianist). Several gramaphone selections were given by Master J. Strange.—The proceeds amounted to £ll.

WESLEY GUlLl).—Last Monday evening in the Wes- leyan Sunday school, Padgate, under the auspices of the above Guild, the Rev. W. Mellor, the resident minister, gave a lecture on " Rome " which was illus- trated by limelight views. There was an excellent attendance. Both the lecture and the limelight views were much appreciated, Mr. Mellor prcving to be an excellent lecturer, his descriptive powers affording his audience considerable delight, whilst the lantern views were of a high class na:ture.

A little time after rumours were circulated that some cause or other the scheme had fallen through.
