div.p: WOMAN'S REALM.
The Examiner, Saturday, November 17, 1906.

div.head: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
div.p: DRESS-FASHION-HOME.
AN EXPER:MENT IN WORK FOR WOMEN.

Several young women are employed in the tracing offices of Messrs. Armstrong at Elswiek, and Captain Lloyd, a director of the company, says they are of the greatest value to them. Their neatness is phenomenal, and they get through their work splendidly. Some of them are under his charge, and he tries to make it a point that they should always appear neatly and nicel34 dressed, for he is persuaded that 60 long as young ladies paid attention to their ap- pearance they would always command respect from the other sex.

div.head: FURS FOR THE WINTER.
div.p: FURS FOR THE WINTER.

OA of the great features of the winter furs will be' the exchange of heavy fur garments for those of lighter design. Most noticeable is this in the tiny fur cravattes, fashioned a the more expensive kind of pelt, and adorned with real lace, that are rapidly taking the place of boas, stoles, and shoulder capes. Fur hats with tulle crowns trimmed with camellias and roses are also a novelty which will be much worn during the next few weeks.

div.head: SMALL GIRL'S COAT.
div.p: SMALL GIRL'S COAT.

The coat sliewn in the illustration is intended for a girl about eight years of age. It is made in a pretty electric-blue shade of frieze. The wide box-pleat .or panel down the front is sup- ported by two pleats on either side; two little epaulettes are carried over each shoulder; and the coat is. caught in round the hips with a

nairow stitched band of the niaterial. The back is arranged in a similar way to the front, the only difference, in fact, being ' that the velvet. covered buttons are omitted. The little mush. room }kat worn with this coat is a dark electric. blue beaver, trimmed with a Paisley scarf, twisted round the crown and knotted at the left side.

div.head: " RITA " AND VOTES FOR WOMEN.
div.p: " RITA " AND VOTES FOR WOMEN.
"Rita" declares that if she were a man sh• would never grant the suffrage to *omen until they had taken "first honours" in the following classes:
"Sensible dressing for the street.' "Economical housekeeping."......
"Sense

"Absolute temperance." "No cigarette smoking." "No gambling or betting." "Rational scheme of education for girls, em- bodying usefulness and the discarding of sense- less accomplishments." "Evenness of temper and the power of logical argument." "No hysterical fads and crazes." "No senseless (imitation of manly sports." FASHIONABLE MUFFS.

Muffs are quite flat and supple this year, and the heads of beasts, birds, and reptiles accepted by beauty as fitting adornment for her person. Birds used to trim smart hats have only small heads and immense tails as a rule, the rest of their anatomy is dispensed with. Some have only the head and two wings, or, perhaps, one. As a rule, says a Globe contributor, these heads could never have belonged to bird, beast, or rep- tile, but are manifestly bogey representations. An owl's head is a very smart thing; we saw one recently with a luxuriant bird of paradise tail tacked on to it which would have considerably astonished the owl. Snakes' heads are among the most approved of, and are used to fasten muff-bags and boas.

div.head: PONGEE SILK EVENING FROCK.
div.p: PONGEE SILK EVENING FROCK.

The evening gown depicted in our illustration might be very' inexpensively realised in pongee silk or some thin muslin-like material, though it is a style that could be made in about any dainty fabric, from glace sirk. downward. The crossover bodice is edged with a strip of fancy gold braid, which continues over each arm, and reappears below the waistbelt in the form of loot ancient end. Two buttons fasten the

bodice where it crosses over, and the open V-shape is filled in with a front of gathered point-d'esprit net, finished off tucker-wise round the top of the low bodice, the tucker effect being continued over the shoulders above the gold band. The little puff sleeves are tucked into a • band of the gold braid just above the elbow, the edge being softened with a suggestion of net frill. The skirt is lone-and full, and is quite devoid of trimming.

div.head: THREE – QUARTER COAT.
div.p: THE THREE - QUARTER COAT.

The three-quarter length tightly -fitting coat seems about the most conspicuous feature of autumn outdoor fashions. It is on the whole a very satisfactory one, says a Globe fashion writer. Of course, women whose slimness of figure is a cherished memory utter the usual plaint that all fashions are for slight figures. So it is, was, and ever will be, we expect. The severely \ plain 'cloth coat, made tightly -fitting, is certainly a test of figure and of good propor- tions that few-women past their girlhood can stand. Also, again, like the majority of fashions, it looks best on tall people. Happily, there are pleasant variations of this garment which suit almost anyone. It can be three-quarter fitting or right in at the back and loose in front, and it can be trimmed in all sorts of ways that humour the figure.

div.head: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.
div.p: TO-DAY'S RECIPE.

CURRIED SWEETBREADS.—AIeIt 2oz. of butter in a stewpan, add one onion sliced, and fry e, golden brown; now stir in loz. of flour and one tablespoonful of curry powder. Simmer till the flour and onions are cooked, and add by degrees three-quarters of a pint of white stock, keeping it well stirred. When the sauce is nice and smooth, put in one clessertspoontill of chutney and one of vinegar. Now add the sweetbreads, cut into pieces 2in. square. Let this stew gently in the sauce for thirty-five minutes. Serve with a border of boiled rice,
MAYOR'S SUNDAY.
OFFICIAL VISIT TO ST. PAUL'S CHURCH.

div.head: Rev. W. Bracecamp and Civic Dignity.
div.p: Rev. W. Bracecamp and Civic Dignity.

In accordance with a time-honoured custom,the newly elected Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) accompanied by members of the Corporation and other public bodies, attended divine service, as a fitting way of inaugurating the municipal year, on Sunday morning. His Worship has long been associated with St. Paul's Church, and it was therefore decided to make the official visit to that Church. The last occasion on which a similar rervice wfts held there was when Alderman Sutton occupied the Mayoral chair. Sunday's procession was one of the largest which has' taken place for many years, repre- sentatives of all shades of political and religious' opinion being present to show their respect for the chief magistrate. At the head was the Volunteer band and next came a large muster of Volunteers,Ambulance Corps, Fire Brigade and Police Force. Preceding the Mayor walked the Mace-bearer (Sergeant Dean) and the , Sword-bearer (Sergeant Bell). His Worship was accompanied by his Chaplain (Rev. W. Bracecamp), the Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle), and the Deputy- Mayor (Alderman Bolton). The members of the Coun- cil and officials in attendance were :—Aldermen Bennett, Evans, Forshaw, Pierpoint, and Tinnion ; Councillors Ashcroft, Ball, Barton, Benson, Cunnington, Clegg, Craik, Dickenson, Duncan, Ellison,Fulton-Smith, Lord, Nield, Sankey, Stott, Skelland, Steel, Wilkinson, Toole, and Wilson; Messrs. A. T. Hallway (deputy town clerk), John Fairhurst (borough treasurer). W. H. Woodcock (assistant treasurer and borough collect° t), F.,Timperley (assistant collector), James Houghton (chits( clerk), Thomas Longdin (borough surveyor),A.M. Her (magistrates' clerk),F. G. Ruddock(public analyst), W. T. Flood (inspector of nuisances), Elijah Place (market inspector), Frank Turner (superintendent of the fire brigate),Robert Young(Cemetery registrar),W.S. Haddock (gas engineer), W.S.Howard (cashier), Charles Madeley (librarian and curator), James Deis (water enginer), James Gray (assistant engineer), F. V. L. Mathias (electrical engineer), J. Moore Murray (director of education) ' • and Messrs. George Pendle- bury (School of Art), E. England (elective auditor),and Firth (Police Court Missionary) ; Board of Guardians, Mrs. Clay, Miss Broadbent, and Messrs. A. J. Jolley, G. Mather, and James Payton ; Education committee, Messrs. G. Walker, A. J. Jolley, and others who are also magistrates ; local magistrates, Messrs. Robert Pierpoint, H. Roberts, R. T. Fairclough, S. Wright, W. Roberts. E. J. Guest, G. Pilling, and W. Richardson ; Aged People's Treat Committee, Messrs. R. Shackleton and Arthur Jolley. The rear was brought up by a large number of townsmen. The Rev. John, Yonge and others joined the procession on its return. On arrival at the church, the procession was met by the wardens (Messrs. J. H. Smethurst and John Rigby), each carrying a staff of office, and the members of the I Bible-class. A large congregation had assembled, seats for the processionists being reserved in the nave. A special form service was conducted by the Chaplain (the Rev. W. Braoecamp) and the Rev. R. B. De Wolf, of Liverpool. The hymns, which were joined in with great heartiness, were "All people that on earth do dwell," "Glorious things of thee are spoken.? "0 God, our help in ages past," and" Onward, Christian soldiers," the 'Volunteer band supplying the accompaniments. Mr. Ernest Wilkes presided at the organ. Prior to the sermon the "bidding prayer" was read. _ .

The Rev. W. BRACECA.IIP took for his text the words "As we have opportunity let us do good unto all men." Galatians vi. 10. He said the Vicar, wardens, church officors,and congregation generally of St. Paul's Church heartily welcomed the Mayor and Corporation of the ancient borough of Warrington to church that morning. It was 19 years since a similar servioe took place there, when the late respected Alderman Sutton was Mayor,and among those whose names were recorded as being present then (with the exception of four), all were dead, emphasizing the fact that whatever their position in life they must all die. The Mayor(Alderman Smethurst) whom the Corporation elected on Friday was well-known to the members of St. Paul's congrega- tion, having worshipped there for the last 30 years. His regular attendance at church, his many acts of self- sacrifice, wee well-known to them. He was a WM whom they all loved and respected, and they felt certain that no man deserved the great honour they had conferred upon him more that he did. They wished him and his good wife, who had always been a real happy year of office. NM lt abelpvmereyet thaopphyim, a very andp roper arrangement that the Corporation should begin their year of office by asking God's blessing upon their work. God ought to be first in all their transactions. The preacher then expounded the text and spoke of (1) the man who murdered his opportunity; (2) the man who just missed his oppor- tunity ; (3) the man who seized his opportunity, and (4) the man who created his opportunity. In conclu- sion,he said,that having spoken to them of what oppor- tunity meant would they allow him to suggest oppor- tunities (apart from the ordinary routine of tbeir office) which they might embrace for the good of the com- munity at large,and for this town in particular? First of all, let him say they had a splendid opportunity of showing to the world that they, at any rate, in Warring- ton recognized the importance of putting the dignity and honour of their office above everything else. He wished he could so instil in their minds that morning that politics ought to have nothing whatever to do with municipal affairs, that they would decide to wipe their hands clean of party feeling. The town, he was sure, i would be with them n this. The very best man, irres- pective of creed, politics, or anything else, ought to be chosen for this position of privilege and responsibility, a man with an irreproachable character, a man whose private life would bear thestrictest investigation. Then they could anticipate that his increased opportunity would be used unselfishly for the benefit of his fellow men. He would show practical sympathy and interest in every cause which had for its object the uplifting of his fellow men. Take, for instance, the society known as the National Service League, which aimed at the improve- ment of the physique and character of the youths in our town, and other towns as well. Let them be men of peace, and the best way to secure peace was to be trained for war. The Housing of the poor was a popular sub- ject just now, but they must be crketul to remember that the remedy for the evil was not in spending large sums of money to build better houses. They must first of all reform the "oharacter, and teach the poor how to live before they would say where they should live. Again some of them had heard of a society known as the Beautiful Warrington Society, which had for its object the beautifying of our streets, open spaces, &c. Let them show their interest, and use their opportunity to make their native town more beautiful, and the people living in it more cheerful and happy. Money and time spent upon work like that must bring credit to themselves and all connected with them. They had heard, too, of a very powerful party growing up in their midst known as the Labour Party—a party which had come to stay. The work that lay befere our country (he did not pay before any one class,for all were equally concerned) was to stimulate the growth of human worth, and to realize, if it be possible, a greater social and human equality—a condition in which no human worth was denied its sphere, and no genius was lost, as it often was, to the world. It was the inevitable next stage of progress. Civil and almost complete political equality had come. It was for them to use their opportunity to encourage this. To bear one anothees burdens, to do to others as they would others should do to theru,to seek first the kingdom of God and His righteousness, these were not merely moral sayings to guide and perfect an individual soul, but they were the only economical and social principles that would bring prosperity to a common- wealth, and these must be the ethical rules and basis of a Labour movement, if it was to be what they hoped it would be to our land. Then further there was the great educational problem. Upon the Council very shortly (if the present Bill became law) would be placed an increased responsibility. Might he just say in reference to this much-vexed and misunderstood subject, it did seem to him that divine commission of our blessed Lord to "Feed my lambs "meant something more than mere secular education. It seemed to him only justice and freedom, to give every parent(the same privilege as they enjoyed) the right of bringing up their children in the same faith as their own, and to enjoy religious liberty, which had always been the pride and glory of the English people. Having appealed for liberal contributions to the offertory on behalf of the Infirmary extension scheme Mr. Braoecamp concluded: Now, brethren, my sincere prayer is that you will try and recognize your opylortunities and privileges more than ever. Go forth to your daily work filled' with the spirit of God. Live the life of a true Christian. ,Go into your Counzil Chamber determining that Christian

div.head: DEBATE ON FEMALE SUFFRAGE.
div.p: DEBATE ON FEMALE SUFFRAGE.

At the usual fortnightly meeting of St. John's Literary and Social Society, held on Tuesday evening, the Hon. President, the Rev. J. L. llilne, 8.D., in the chair, a debate took place on the question " Should women have the franchise ? " Mr. Lewsey, in opening for the affirmative, said the question was an important and interesting one. With each extension of the fran- chise civilization had made enormous strides forward, and there had been great moral and social improvement of the masses. He asserted that the full franchise should be granted to women, not for any particular reason but for every reason. Some women had asked for it, and others were prepared to fully use their powers when they got them. Woman had become a wage earner, a producer, and an educational factor. Had not the worker for wages a right to send her representative to see justice dokto her ? That women's work was daily increasing was a vital reason for the extension of the franchise to them. Women attended political assemblies, occupied seats of honour on the platform, worked in every way open to them, and virtually won numbars of seats for their husbands, brothers or sweet- hearts, thus proving that they understood politics much better than men gave theca credit for. There were 1,030 women acting as Poor Law Guardians, and hun- dreds on District Cauncils. It was not far from the platform to the ballot-box or from the Board of Guardians to the House of Commons. There was a woman's influence in the educational world where she had a far greater share in the educating of the young ' than men had. Woman's great and indispensable work commenced at home but that was no proof that it must end there. Woman was the weaker sex only in the unimportant sense of physical endurance and strength. In all other moral and intellectual qualities, such as strength of mind, affection, patience, perse- verance in well-doing, parception of right from wrong, mo 1 stability, hatred of injustice, and ri unselfish xvo k for humanity, woman was the stronger sex. When women would be seen with men working for the uplifting of society, the abolition of vice and the righting of all wrongs, then they should see a quicker solution of all social problems, and the dawn of the day when God's will would be done on earth as it was done in Heaven.

The leader for the negative said the question was one which ought to be treated in a practical manner. No logical case could be made out for female suffrage. All forms of government were based on force, and the will of the nation as expressed in its laws must be the will of those who had had the physical power to enforce it. The most important of all reasons why the franchise should not be granted to women was simply that women didn't want it. That was at once is safe practical and statesmanlike way of dealing with the matter. Mr. Asquith, a stateman of experience and responsibility, showed that he was fully alive to this serious aspect of tbe question when, in reply to a deputation of women that waited upon him, he said, that the price they (the women) might have to pay for the franchise might be "the putting in jeopardy of the status, the position, the real authority and the unique influence of women as a whole in the community." Women now exercised a great power and influence in the home, in the family Me, and in the social life of the community, and that was the sphere in which an all-wise Providence had meant her to make her influence felt. He contended that women workers would not be helped by the franchise. Woman's drawback in the labour world was her inability to combine on trade union lines as successfully as men. Legally women's interests were well looked after now, and the marriage and other laws greatly favoured her. That woman had votes for local governing bodies was no argument that she should have the parliamentary franchise. The local authority had much to do I do with what concerned the home, while the poor law institution and the elementary school were to some extent the home on a larger stale. Let them consider well before they dragged women, and dragged them against their will into the bitter strife of party politics. Let them ask whether the result would be to the advan- tage either of women themselves or of mankind generally. A vigorous discussion followed the remarks of the two leaders, and on the vote being taken the affirmative was carried by a large majority.

div.head: Shorthand Writers' Association.
div.p: Shorthand Writers' Association.

The weekly meeting af the above was held at the Winmarleigh Cafe on Wednesday night, a fair number of members being present. After speed practice, Mr. J. W. Box gave an interesting lecture entitled " The uses of fitAion." Several books of modern fiction received somewhat severe criticism at the hands of the Lecturer, who made a very able comparison between the writers of a few generations ago and those of the present day. Allusion was made to the good that had been done, from time to time, by the exposnre, by various authors, of public and other institutions which were wceftilly mismanaged, and of very preva- lent evils winch existed in our midst, and also by the advocating of reforms which were urgently needed. Reference was also made to the works of such outhors as Jules Verne, who had foreshadowed the innovation of many of our recent inventions, notably the sub- marine, airship, etc. The Lecturer said he felt sure that the reading of good works of fiction assisted us in forming loftier ideals. Mr. Box handled his subject extremely well, and an enjoyable discussion ensued, to which he briefly. replied. A hearty vote of thanks to the Lecturer concluded the meeting, A shorthand library has now been formed in connection with the Association, and several Members have contributed books, etc., printed in Phonography. Mr.J.P. Hadson has been appointed hon. librarian, and it is expected that this adjunct of the Association's work will be taken full advantage of, as the reading of shorthand is quite as important to the shorthand student as practice in writing.

div.head: DRINK TRAFFIC.
div.p: THE DRINK TRAFFIC.
QUESTION OF DISINTERESTED MANAGEMENT DISCUSSED.
Speech By Mr. C. E. Parker.

" Is the introduction of a system of disinterested management of the drink trade desirable in this country" was the question under discussion at a meeting held in Bewsey-road Wesleyan Lecture Hall on Monday evening in connection with the Wesley Guild. Great interest was taken in the proceedings and there was a crowded attendance. The Rev. Sidney Pitt presided. Mr. C. E. PARKER opened the debate in the affirma- tive. He pointed out that the question arose from a recommendation in the report of Lord Peel's commission and the consequence had been the formation of a Temperance League. The main idea which permeated the work of that organization was a recognition of the fact that adult teetotalers numbered only about one in ten of the population and that if anything practical was to be accomplished an effort must be made to enlist the moral support of people who were as decent as any teetotaler but who were not prepared to take the position of total abstinence. The League's policy included the establishment of a time limit—with which they would all agree—(hear, hear)—and until the expira- tion of that limit an increase of the compensation levies so that the magistrates would have a larger fund to be applied to the extinction of licences. Other proposals were that local authorities should have more ample power in dealing with the drink traffic, that there should be shorter hours and Sunday closing, and that ' places of recreation and social intercourse to counter- act the influence of the public house, should be estab- lished. Disinterested management, which was advocated by the Commission, was a very vital point. It meant that those who had charge of the sale of the drink I should not be interested in that sale. Under the present system two influences were brought together—the ! depraved appetite of the man or woman for drink, and the lust for gain on the part of the vendor of intoxicants. Those were about two of the worst influences they could bring together. The sug- gestion was that the municipalities should have power within their areas to hand over to a body of men who cared to undertake the task, the management of all or a proportion of the public houses ; the idea being that these men, for philanthropic reasons to some extent, should provide the money necessary to equip and manage the public houses that they should receive interest on their investment at the rate of 5 per cent., and that any profits over that amount should be given to some public object. He thought it would certainly be a danger if the profit went to reducing the rates— (hear, hear)—and he did not know that any municipality would be so degraded as to push the sale of drink for the sake of lessening the rates. It would, however, be a great gain if the stimulus which was at present given to the sale of drink for private profit were removed and the traffic placed in the hands of those to whom it would be of no advantage to push the sale. Suppose for instance that a garden suburb was developed in Warrington, the question of providing facilities for obtaining intoxicants would arise. He contended I that it would be better for the house to be in the hands of some parties who would be willing to subscribe for 1 its erection and equipment and who would have no interest in the sale of drink. He believed that if municipalities were allowed to try the experiment and work the system in the best possible way, it would be a I great advance in temperance reform. They must recognise that even if they got local option passed to-morrow it would perhaps not be effective in more than one in twenty places. What, were they to do in the others? Were they going to stand still and do I nothing to stop the excesses ? He thought dis- interested management would have a very good effect and it had his entire approval. (Applause.) Mr. I Parker then moved that the meeting express the view I that disinterested management is desirable.

Mr. J. T. ROWLANDS took up the opposition and contended that there should be no parleying with such an evil as the drink traffic. What they wanted was local veto, and statistics proved that in the villages and small townships of Norway and Sweden where this reform bad been adopted, the inhabi- tants had been happy and comfortable. The Feathers' Hotel was an instance of the municipality being interested in a public-house, and they now saw that it was in the hands of the brewers. Mr. Rowlands strongly condemtfed political clubs, and concluded by urging his hearers not to have anything to do with such schemes as disinterested management, but to fight the drink curse until England was freed from it. (Applause.) Mr. J. UPSON supported the resolution and said Mr. Rowlands had made no suggestion as to practical reform which would remedy the ill-effects of the drink traffic. As to his attack on clubs he (Mr. Upson) was a member of the Liberal Club and the Manchester Press Club, and in neither of those institutions had he seen anything which would lead him to say they were places where drink was largely taken. He was informed that at the Liberal Club which had some hundreds of mem- bers, the drink consumed was one barrel (30 gallons) per week. How anyone could say that such a place was on all fours with a public house,he did not know. With their usual conservatism, the Englisli people were only just beginning to study the question and to think of it as other people had been thinking of it for twenty-five years. Our colonies and continental nations had been for twenty-five years scientifically studying the question and were convinced that the methods advocated by the United Kingdom alliance were impracticable, and that while such methods might be a counsel of perfection it was absolutely necessary to do something in the meantime to restrict the evil. Since the introduction of the Gothenburg system in 1876 the consumption of spirits in Norway and Sweden had decreased by two- thirds as compared with what it was in 1850. New Zealand and gleensland had had local option with very poor results. If that was the case with countries of advanced thought, where social reforms had made tremendous strides, was it conceiv- able that in a country like ours, with its long traditions and social habits and vested interests in the traffic, that we would get the population of any locality to say they would have no drink sold within their boundaries ? He maintained that there was not a local authority in the Kingdom that would permit the abolition of the sale of drink within its area. He contended it would be a step forward to Lake the traffic out of the hands of those who made profit by it. (Applause). Dr. FERGUSON said that disinterested management, if successful, would be only a paliative. Prohibition must be their coal an -I until they attained it they would have nothing like sobriety in this country. (Applause). Mr. GORDON PITT Said local veto was a desideratum but he did not think any community would accept it. He therefore advocated disinterested managemet as an improvement. The discussion was continued by Messrs. SEED, NORMAN and others. Mr. PARKER in reply said he did not say disinterested 'management would work a tremendous revolution but it would be a good thing and he therefore considered that where it could be utilized it would be wrong for a temperance man to oppose it. The attitude which some people adopted of refusing the assistance of moderate drinkers. was in his view unfortanate. The benefits they had received in the way of temperance legislation hod been largely due to the fact that many decent tpeople who were not total abstainers had stood by the ltemperance party and demanded reforms. He hoped that meeting would have the result of awakening the emperance sentiment of Warrington which had too one been asleep. (ap p lause.) I On a vote being taken the resolution declaring that 'disinterested management is desirable was carried by 132 votes to 26.

div.head: EXAMINEE.
div.p: THE EXAMINEE.
NOVEMBER 17th 1906.

With regard to the ques- SLAVERY AND tion of Chinese labour, SHAME, matters have now reached boiling point on the benches below the gangway in the House of Commons, and ev3n on the seats behind the Treasury bench. This was evident on Wednesday, when Mr. R, C. LEHMANN rose to move the adjournment on " definite matter of urgent public importance." A thrill is said to have gone through the House Everybody knew what Mr. LEHNIAIVN meant. He is a man of fearless character. A change in his relations t.) "Punch," to which periodical he was and is a principal contri- butor, was brought about by his. outspokenness regarding the events which led up to the South African War. A brief editorship of a London daily newspaper of importance was brought to an end for not wholly dissimilar reasons. Mr' LEHMANN is a man who will not compromise, but he is only one of many members of Parliament who believe, reasonably or otherwise, that the Government has been far from swift and , decisive enough in its methods of dealing with the Chinese question. He is, too,one of those—and this means the vastly preponderating bulk of the Liberal party —who will not compromise whatever on the subject of Chinese serfdom in the Transvaal, and who would be all the less disposed to compromise if that were possible, after the receipt by the Government of Mr. BuCKNILL'S terrible and shock- ing report. The position of the Government is undoubtedly one of great difficulty. No Govern rnent can do just what it likes to do, nor do always at the moment what it means to do in the long run. It is hampered by all sorts of considers - times of State, by the necessity of adjusting every sort of change to existing conditions, so as to pro- duce the least dislocation, by considerations of finance, of the position of officials, and, in this

instance, of how to place the burden on the shoulders by which it ought to be borne. The present Transvaal evil is of such magnitude that it is merely natural that those who are free from the responsibilities of statesmanship should desire at once to pluck it up by the roots. Allow. ance must also be made for some uuavoidable exasperation at the manner in which the Govern- ment has been openly and insolently thwarted in the interests of the importers of Chinese slaves. Almost the last act of Mr. LYTTLETON as Colonial Secretary was to authorise the issue of permits for the importation of sixteen thousand additional Chinamen. One of the latest acts of Lord SELBORNE has been to throw his influence on the side of Mr.PEncy FITZPATIEK, one of the pro-Chinese. The Government ought, in our opinion, to have struck a pen through the permits so shamelessly issued. It ought to have taken strong measures with Lord SELBORNE immediately on the publication of his letter to the MAYOR OF PRETORIA. The Administration has seemed to move slowly and decisively where rapid and ruthless action appeared to be called for by the situation, and that is why Mr. LEHMANN pro- posed to move the adjournment of the House on Wednesday,and why he returned to the attack on Thursday with unanswerable evidence of the nature of the confidential report which has been received at the Colonial Office. The facts were officially admitted and there was no mistaking the stern temper of the House though Mr. WINSTON Carmen= made a brilliant speech in which he deprecated hasty action on the "impulse of repugnance or anger." Mr. Orroncurrr. was candid, however, and unhesitating in the assurances he was prepared to give. In a short time, he said, Chicese labour would be eradicated "on the authority of a South African Parliament," and he added solemnly that "this system must absolutely, utterly, and totally come to a close." With these assurances, admirably supported by the Prime Minister, the House was satisfied. We are, at last, within measurable distance of seeing South Africa cleansed of the foul blot, the responsi- bility for which was thrust upon this country by the late Conservative Government of unhappy memory.

The Trades Council, the PAUPER LABOUR. Board of Guardians, and finally the Magistrates,have all found it necessary to adjudicate on the case of the man Clarke, who was taken from the Work- house by a Guardian, employed at 6d. an hour for 39 hours, and then left his work and returned to the Workhouse. A pretty problem has been pre- sented. The Trades Council was righteously 1 indignant at the man, who was a painter, being paid only 6d. an hour instead of the standard wage for his trade. The Guar- dians prosecuted him for failing to maintain himself when he had work to do—even at 6d. an hour—and the magistrates sent him to prison for the nominal term of one day. The moral of the case is not very obvious, unless it be that a Guardian is ill-advised in taking a man from the shelter of the Workhouse to work at anything less than the standard rate of wage. This stan- dard wage question is somewhat of a bug- bear. Apparently the most charitably disposed I amongst us will not be allowed to find a man a "job "unless we are willing to pay more, perhaps, than the work is worth. If we take a man " off the road" and set him to painting the shop-front we shall not ask the Trades Council how much we ought to pay him even if he be an RA, and his standard wage is £5 an hour. Of course, the cases are not exactly on all fours,but Mrs. Clay thought she was doing tb9 man a good turn by finding him work at a living wage. Her mistake was in taking pauper labour direct from a public institu- tion like the Workhouse. As a sequel to the LATCHFORD'S electoral struggle in Latch - AFTERMATH. ford Ward on November ht, there has been an e n outburstth3 toifhleerter N- werei nrga dbi eat; e ee nn dp sides, most of which has found its h i allch is s wtr aCoanmoYcni ens,i eentrnthvotea thermtei ve i press. On our eighth page, en • lettersth e fig hfight which w tfhe Non-Trading mq bearuri.tepe more aoedrde serm extensivealed es nadirectlydefence ceoun ptfooofr l no principle in Latchford. If the public did not quite understand the position of affairs in Latchford on the day of the election they should be thoroughly enlightened by now. The acceptance by the Mayor's auditor (Councillor Wilson) of £3O remuneration was a direct contravention of the principle which the bulk of the Warrington burgesses have affirmed viz., that' no man shall I profit directly by his membership of the Town Council, and we are afraid the moral significance of the matter was not properly grasped by the 1660 burgesses of Latchford, or they would not have returned Mr. Wilson. The version of the matter which carried most weight with the unthinking rortion of the electorate was that Mr. Wilson was a poor man, he had done the work, and why should he not have the money ? This was an ingenious appeal to the Britishers' sense of justice and it was made the most of by the opponents of the Non-Trading cause and the partizan Conservatives.. As the result of the ventilation it has since had the inwardness of the question at issue is better understood, and the Non-Trading standpoint vindicated. In kid correspondence with Mr. Dodds the chairman of the Conservative Association, Mr. W. Peter Rylands, who backed up C Wilson on the day of the election, candidly admits that "it would be better that no payments should be made to any member of the CJrporation for , work done for the Corporation," and suggests the selection of a Mayor's Auditor outside the council. This is, unfortunately, impossible and we believe that Councillor Wilson has already been re-appointed to the post. Presumably he will once again accept the fee which the Corporation pays under the Public Health Act. If he does he must expect the legality of his position to be challenged at once. At the same time he will, we conclude from Mr. Ry!ands' remarks, Is) him- self open to the censure of the Chairman of the Conservative Association, of which body he is the nominee.

We regret that the President of the Liberal Association, in entering into the public debate of the question, has taken the opposite view to the leader of the Conservatives, There can be no question after five years of the most strenuous and sell-sacrfficing labour, that the object of the Non-Traders is solely aud simply the securing of absolute purity in municipal life. Such an object ought to be in the forefront of Liberal ideals so long as the party concerns itself with mucicipal affairs. On the contrary, the official Liberal attitude has, all along, been inimical to the Non- Trading cause. There has, in fact, been more sympathy on the side of the party which is not usually considered the party of progress, and that sympathy with the Non-Trading ideal has been avowed openly now by the Conservative ex-member for the Borough and the Chairman of the Conservative Association. The official Liberals, indeed,seem to be at variance even with their own Mernebr, Mr. A. H. Crosfield, M.P., who has, like the two Tory leaders expressed himself in favour of the main Non-Trading prin- ciple. So long as this is the case we see little prospect of the unity in Liberal ranks for which the President makes so strong a plea. We have ventured to say before that we think the policy of the Liberal party in regard to municipal matters has been an altogether wrong one and we think so still. It has been said by the man whO did more to win the Parliamentary election in Warrington than anyone else that "the Liberals ought to be the Non-Traders," and that IPS m we believe, the auto and substance of the whole [natter.

It is a healthy sign when TEMPERANCE such a keen interest is REFORM. taken in temperance reform as was manifested in Mon- day evening's debate at Bewsey-road on "The disinterested management of public-houses." pi progress is to be made n the fight against the devastating evil of the drink traffic, temperance workers must keep themselves well informed on every fresh development of the question and be prepared to give calm consideration to suggested reasonable measures of reform. One of the most recent proposals, which has given rise to considerable discussion and formed the subject of Monday's debate, emanates from the Temperance League. It is that local authorities should have the power to hand over the manage- ment of public-houses to a body of disinterested sentle.men,who would be prepared to invest money in their equipment and who would receive interest at the rata of not more than 5 per cent. Any profit which remained over that amount would be devoted to some deserving local object. The scheme will probably not commend itself to many ardent prohibitionists who believe that "disinterested management" would only complicate the situation and make the campaign against the drink traffic all the more difficult, in as much as it would not then be a straight conflict with the brewing industry. If something immediately practical can be accom- plished, however, the innovation is worthy of a trial. As Mr. C. E. Parker pointed out " disinter- ested management " would be infinitely preferable to the present system by which two of the worst influences—the craving for intoxicants and the lust for monetary gain—are brought together. Disinterested management would, we believe, be a step—if only a short one—in the right direction and it behoves temperance advocates not to stand in the way of anything which might help to lessen a great evil.

Extremely interesting are THE PREVENTION the results of the calcula- oF RAILWAY tions which have been made ACCIDENTS, to determine at what rate of speed,relatively, an engine Must overturn in going round a curve. Of course, the sweep of the curve is the first determining factor, next to that the speed ; but they are not all. The Salisbury disaster has set civil engineers and college mathematicians at work. Assuming there were no secondary influences to take into account, it was found that the speed at which, theoretically, an engine would over-balance at this point was sixty-seven and a half miles per hour. But there are other causes, which reduce the probable rate to sixty-six miles, or less. The gyration or "spin" of the wheels—the gyrostatic action—gives them a tendency to "refuse" curves, and go right on. Here the gyrostatic effect was calculated to make the engine tilt up from the inner rail when the speed was a mile less I than would he possible if there were no gyrostatic action to consider. An error of an inch in the height of the centre of gravity when the engine was constructed would reduce the critical speed by another half inch, while the balance weights used in the reciprocating locomotive, at certain parts of the stroke, tend to lift the engine above the :ails. The " Times" engineering supplement gives some wise conclusions upon these points. There will be a growing tendency to straighten out curves ; in dark and light its maximum speed must be advertised to the driver at every curve ; the means possessed by drivers for measuring speed need revision ; and speed records must be registered automatically at given stations and inspected by the Board of Trade. The measure- ment and control of speeds, it now seems to be pretty certain, will have to be more exactly under- taken.

" We would rather teach the children that the local tradesman who takes an interest in municipal affairs is a hero to be saluted in the streets than teach the children the patriotism of the toy rifle, the goose step, and the waving banner.—" Christian World." * A decidedly smart answer was given in the witness box at Runcorn Police Court by P.C. Hulse when asked " Who is to judge whether or not a man is drunk ?" Witness promptly replied " The landlord judges. The police judge. The magistrates decide.'' Promotion ought to await the constable who is so quick at repartee. * * The members of the Warrington Trades and Labour Council are apparently somewhat indifferent as to the abolition of corporal punishment in schools, and it was only after Mr. Podmore bad used considerable persuasion that on Tuesday evening they agreed to entertain (a month hence) a letter from the Society for the Reform of School Discipline. A similar motor fatality has occurred ,near Chester to the one which happened on the Bolcbroad near , Warrington a year or two ago. On Tuesday night a gentleman and two ladies ran over a man who was , lying on the roadside and killed him. We suppose, that, once again, it was drink which was directly the cause of the unfortunate man choosing the high road as his couch for the night. * * One of the noteworthy incidents connected with this week's " sitting " of Parliament is that Mr. J. Tomkinson, M.P. for Crewe, who does not claim to be considered a young man, began the day early with six hours' hunting in Cheshire, then occupied four , hours in travelling to London, and went straight to the House of Commons for fourteen hours, thus com- pleting the twenty-for hours. * * * " The Gardeners' Chronicle "for November 10, has an article on " Odontoglossums at Warrington " which' speaks in highly flattering terms of the orchids grown by Alderman Bolton at Wilderspool. In the introduc- tory paragraph is a rather amusing sample of intelligent anticipation." The owner of the plants is referred to as " William Bolton, Esq., the popular Mayor of Warrington for probably the fourth year in auceession." Someone has been counting the orchids before they have flowered! * * The Committee of the Manchester Peace Society contemplate holding a public meeting at Warrington chiefly to counteract the powerful influence of the _National Service League in the town." The Society believes that the militarising of the nation instead of leading to peace will inevitably lead to war. The ocal branch of the Learnie has been particularly active in its propaganda work, and we welcome the proposal ' o inaugurate a campaign against this proposed 'nation in arms. *s* There are some good things in this week's " Tatter." One full-page picture illustrates the best joke we have come across for some time. Scene: A London thoroughfare during the laying of wood. blocks. Small girl (who has just purchased a pram- full of wood-blocks from one of the workmen), " Call that a pennuth, why yer can still see the bloomin' kid." So you can in the picture, but the" kid "looks very unhappy in the midst of its uncomfortable sur- roundings,

* * *. Another item sets forth tte following" soapological " problem : " Let the Lever, M.P.. of the first-class, , balance about a point such that a weight of 15oz. at ( one end will be equal to a pound at the other. Now if the constituents of M.P. meet in A, or make A. of , the place where they meet, and the reaction SO be ~ opposite to the action of the Lever, and the explana- tion of M.P. be only SO, SO, prove that equilibrium mill be restorecr,to the figure SOAP when the Lever is to longer M.P."

I' I hope this meeting will have the effect of awaken- Ing the temperance sentiment of Warrington which has been too long asleep" was Mr. C. E. Parker's Observation at the debate held at Bewsey-road Wesley Guild meeting on Monday. We heartily re-echo the sentiment, for few towns can offer a wider scope for earnest temperance effort. Meanwhile such meetings as that held on Monday are distinctly encouraging.
I

The members showed themselves to be particularly well informed on the question and, as Mr. Parker remarked,, a true temperance ring pervaded the proceedings. fi 0 o We have all become so accustomed to the repre- sentation of" St. George and the Dragon" on certain coins of the realm, that probably few people trouble about the details of the design. Major-General Bland Strange, however, in his speech at the National Service League meeting, offered sundry pointed criticisms. lie spoke contemptuously of St. George's short sword which he likened to a cheese knife, and said his only protective armour was exactly that which he did not need—a helmet. The average Englishman, however, is not a stickler for accuracy in these little matters, so long as the coin is worth its face value.

*s* A well-deserved and pointed rebuke was adminis- tered to the dignitaries of the State Church on Thurs- day by Mr. Winston Churchill when speaking in reply to Mr. R. C. Lenmann's motion on the horrible dis- closures concerning the South African compounds. He said, "when I see bishops and archbishops hurry- ing into the field to ask the Government to take action I ask Why this belated intervention ?" When the late Government first authorised Chinese labour in defiance of Liberal, Labour, and Nonconformist pro- tests, was it not the Primate himself who alluded to the hated ordinance as " a regrettable necessity ?" * * There is such a unanimity of opinion among Liberals as to the necessity for ending or mending the House of Lords, that there was a difficulty in raising any serious opposition at Monday evening's debate in con- nection with the Junior Liberal Association. Several members were deputed at the last moment to argue for the retention of the Second Chamber in its present form but they could only put forward a weak case. The verdict of the meeting was overwhelmingly in favour of the abolition of hereditary legislators. It would be better if in the future subjects on which there is a divergence of opinion,even in Liberal ranks, were selected. The debate would certainly gain in , interest.

We are sure that trade unionists will strongly repudiate such an attack on Mr. Havelock Wilson, M.P., as was made upon him on Sunday by Mr. Charles Duncan, M.P. for Barrow-in-Furness. In face of Mr. Wilson's noble services on behalf of seamen,this critic had the temerity to suggest that Middlesborough would some day return a "Labour man" and on being taken to task by his audience proceeded to belittle Mr. Wilson's work. We are glad to see that the Trade Union members on the ministerial side of the House of Commons have passed a resolution expressing deep regret at Mr. Duncan's attack and placing on record "its emphatic opinion that Mr. Wilson's efforts during the discussion on the Merchant Shipping Bill have been characterised by indomitable courage under trying physical conditions, and by much skill as a Parliamentarian, several' special concessions having thus been obtained by him for the seamen." Young men interested in politics are invited to form a society for the systematic study of everyday political questions, by means of debates, reading circles, &c. During the past few months several strong societies have been formed in the principal Lancashire and Cheshire towns (including Warrington) for the further- ance of these objects. These societies are connected with the Lancashire and Cheshire Association, which is in turn affiliated with the Young British Liberals' Federation. Runcorn and District has supported Liberalism heartily in the past,and ought to be able to support a strong society. If there is any young man in the Northwich or Eddisbury division who would like to enter into active work on behalf of Liberalism, he should immediately communicate either with the Hon. Secretary, J. W. Bogle, 398 Stockport-road, Bredbury, or with F. Godwin Lloyd, Hon. Treasurer, Lancashire and Cheshire Association, 12, Stockport road, Man- chester.

* * A conference of motorists was held in London on Wednesday to consider prospective legislation. A number of suggestions were embodied in resolutions, among them being condemnation of any general speed limit and approval of revenue obtained from motor taxation being expended on the improvement of roads. With the abolition of the speed limit we do not agree. There are too many "road-hogs" already, and if there were no legal limit to speed they would practically run riot in some parts of the country. A good case can be made out for the second resolution and motorists have a right to claim that some of the revenue—if not all —from the taxation of automobiles should be expended on the maintenance and improve- ment of the roads. Mr. W. Runciman, M.P., Parlia- mentary Secretary to the Local Government Board, explained that the idea of basing taxation of cars on horse-power had been abandoned, ond the Board would welcome suggestions from the Motor Union for a just scale of taxation. They would then soon fix the amount.

PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LA.NCISHIRE.--AdVt. Stern Father Sued. At the Warrington County Court on Thursday, before his Honour Judge Shiress Will, K.C., Thomas Carr, an Irishman, claimed £2 16s. from Richard Hodson, farmer, Rixton Moss, near Warrington, being £1 harvest money alleged to have been agreed to be paid by defendant to the plaintiff, and one week's wages 18s., and one week's wages in lien of notice 18s.—Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff and Mr. Steel defended.—Plaintiff's case was that he was engaged by the defendant as a labourer, at wages of 188. per week and he was also promised £1 harvest money. One Saturday night defendant saw plaintiff taking his daughter home and on the following Monday morning discharged him without paying him.—Defendant denied that there was any arrangement as to harvest money and said it had not been his practice to pay any for the past eleven years.—His Honour decided that there was no agreement for the payment of harvest money and gave judgment for plaintiff for 365. wages. S, GARLAND, Builders' Ironmonger, &c., 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. The Catholic Young Men's Society. The annual general meeting of this society took place on Friday evening last, Councillor Owen Toole presiding.—The Chairman, in his opening remarks, congratulated the society on the position they had attained, and the prestige they had gained during the past year. They had made their presence felt during the municipal elections in no small manner, and he thanked them for their having so ardently worked for his return to the Town Council on November Ist. —Father Roche then addressed the members. The furthering of Catholic interests in civic and social life was, he said, peculiarly adapted to the members of , the C.Y.M.S. of Great Britain, and much was expected I of theni. He congratulated the Warrington branch onl the start they had made, but warned them to keep up the work they had commenced, and never let their position be weakened. Peter Delaney ; hon. treasurer, Bro. James Boyle; hon. sec. Bro. H. McMullen; hon, corresponding secretary, Bro. A. M. Crowe. The society held their annual church parade on Sunday to St. Mary's, Latchford. An Unsuccessful Oil Venture. An unusual case was heard at the Warrington County Court on Thursday by his Honour Judge Shiress Will, K.C., when Samuel Perrin, Lymm, sued James Higginson and William Henry Phillips,of Irlam and Cadishead, for ,£32 cash alleged to have been advanced at their request. Mr. Unsworth appeared for plaintiff, Mr. Butterworth (Rochdale) for Phillips, while Higginson was unrepre- sented.—Mr. Unsworth said plaintiff who was 70 years of age was an illiterate labourer and his son worked for the defendants. Higginson was an undis- charged bankrupt and he knew a secret process for the refining of oil. Phillips was a company promoter or at all events was a man who speculated in the formation of companies. On October 27th, 1905, Phillips -and Higginson entered into an agreement by which Phillips was to find cash to put down plant for the refining of oil and to get it on the market with a view, to forming the concern into a limited liability com- pany and then selling it. Under that agreement Higginson was to have £3 per week and Phillips was to find the money, in the first instance to the amount of .050. Premises were taken at Cadishead and leased in the joint names of Higginson and Phillips. The oil was put on the market in December 1905, and things seemed to so on all right until May 1906, when Phillips told Higginson that he could find no more money to buy raw oil to be refined. After discussion as to what should be done, Higginson proposed to find some money. He went to Perrin, who on a pre- vious occasion had procured his release from gaol by advancing £23, and borrowed £B2 —practically plain- tiff's life savings. The money had never been repaid, and the plant and effects had been sold up and realized £9O. It was contended that as Perrin's money had, been used in the business, Phillips was equally liable with Higginson.—Evidence was then called, the witnesses including the defendant Higginson who said Phillips knew he was borrowing the money and every halfpenny was used in the busi- ness. He denied that the money was borrowed to pay off his (Higginson's) own debts.—Phillips' defence was that he lost the £550 which he invested in the concern, and in March he ceased finding any money. Higginson had been carrying on some business of his own at the place, and the was devoted entirely to his own purposes. Plfillips was not a company pro- moter. He gave no authority for the borrowing of the money.—His Honour held the evidence to show that the money went into the business, and gave judgment against both defendants for the amount claimed with costs.

Mr. A. IL Crosfield, M.P. Mr. Crosfield's health, we regret to say, is still not altogether satisfacory. and he has been strongly advised t 3 take a couple of months complete rest from business and politics It is hoped however, it may be unnecessary for him to do so before the end of the Session.

Beamont School Fees. The Education Committee has received a letter from the Board of Education, stating that, as at present advised, they cannot consent to the charge of fees at the Beamont Council School, and the Finance Committee gave instructions for a reply to be sent to the Board with a view to their re-consideration of the request. The Education Committee will meet on Monday to discuss the matter.

04rls' Sad Downfall. A sad case was heard at the Borough Court, yester- day, when two respectably dressed girls, Jessie Clarke (18), St. Helens, and Phoebe Glover (15), Warrington, were charged with theft. It appeared that the girls, who had been hawking plants, secured lodgings with Mr. John Stockton, Gas-street, from whose house they stole a gold watch, two silver watches, a pair of gold ear-rings and other articles of a total value of 10s. The elder girl was fined 40s. whilst a conviction was recorded against Glover, who was handed over to the care of the Police Court Missionary.

There will be music at 7.30, followed by a whist drive commenc- ing at 8 o'clock and lasting until 10.30. After an interval for supper, the assembly room will be cleared for dancing, which will continue until 1.30 to the strains of a military band. div.head: EDELSTEN ACTION. CORPORATION DECIDE TO SETTLE.
div.p: THE EDELSTEN ACTION. CORPORATION DECIDE TO SETTLE.
Council Meeting Last Night.

The action pending between Mr. Edelsten and the Corporation respecting the purchase of the Mersey Works is to be settled. This was decided upon at a special meeting of the Town Council last evening when it was resolved :—" That the Town Clerk be authorised to settle the action of Edelsten v. the Corporation of Warrington and William Bolton by undertaking to carry out the agreement of 3rd Decem- ber, 1004, made between John Arther Edelsten and William Bolton for tlic sale of premises in Knutsford- road, Warrington, known as the Mersey Works, and that he be authorised to pay costs, as taxed between party and party, of the plaintiff. And that the common seal be affixed to any necessary agreement."

The resolution was opposed by the Non-Traders, Councillor Pemberton moving an amendment that it be not confirmed. He contended that in face of the fact that Counsel had advised that the Corporation had a good case, they i had no right to vote away the rate- payers' money n costs. Councillor Lonn seconded.
The voting was as' follows : For the amendment : Councillors Skelland, Ashcroft, Lord,' Pemberton, Cunnington, Wilding and Chantler-7.

Against : Aldermen Tinnion, Forshaw, Evans : Councillors Fulton-Smith, Wilkinson, Toole, Sankey, Ellison, Dr. Joseph, Steel, Ball, Nield, Wilson, Barton, Clegg, Stott, and the Mayor-17. The amendment was therefore lost.
Prior to the Council meeting, the matter had been thoroughly thrashed out in General Purposes Com- mittee which lasted two hours.

div.head: MR JOHN S. GREEN'S AFFAIRS. Five Years' Misery.—Judge's Sympathy.
div.p: MR JOHN S. GREEN'S AFFAIRS. Five Years' Misery.—Judge's Sympathy.

The story of a disastrous business enterprise was told to Mr. Lereshe, sitting as deputy, at the Manchester County Court yesterday morning, when John Shaw Green, journalist, formerly of Warrington, applied for his discharge in bankruptcy. Green was filling a position as editor when, in ISA he met a Mr. William Skilling, of Lymm, the proprietor of five suburban newspapers, circulating between South Manchester and Knutsford, and subse- quently entered into partnership with him, giving up his own editorship. He put £350 into the business, taking a hall-share, also agreeing to take upon himself one-half of a sum of £l5O Mr. Skilling owed to his printers, the New Cheshire County News, Limited. The relations of the partners, said the report of Mr. Gibson, the Official Receiver, became strained almost from the first, and ultimately Green served Mr. Skilling with notice of dissolution Of partnership. Meanwhile, the "County Newsy' sued the firm for the £l5O, and, having obtained judgment, proceeded for a receiving order, which was made in 1901. A first and final dividend of 10s. 10d. in the £ was paid. Applicant alleged that he was misled as to profits, Szc. Mr. Gibson said the applicant had been most unfor- tunate, being only four mouths in the business and not drawing a single penny from it. Now, without having committed any commercial irregularity, he was before , the Court as a bankrupt, his private fortune wrecked. In granting an immediate discharge, subject to a judgment for the nominal sum of £lO, his Honour said great sympathy was to be felt towards the applicant. Applicant : I have lost my money, and I have had five years' misery.'

div.head: LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: LOCAL CHURCHES.
Young Free Churchmen's Auxiliary.

At a meeting of the above organization last evening the Rev. John Yonge read a highly interesting paper on "The Life of Gladstone." He dealt specially with Mr. Gladstone's attitute on the disestablishment of the Irish Church and the Education Act of 1870, as being matters of particular interest to Free Churchmen. He also quoted from correspondence of the " Grand Old Man" with Mr. Bright showing that Mr. Gladstone was not averse to a secular solution of the education question. Mr. Yonge was cordially thanked for his address.

MAN DROWNED AT WIDNES..

The body of an unknown man was recovered from the Mersey near Widnes Dock on Sunday evening. A woman named Bertha Tomlinson saw deceased near Gossage's Quay, and they walked together till they got to the dock gates. Mrs. Tomlinsoncrossed the gates first, and when a little ahead she heard a splash and a cry for help. She gave the alarm, and the body was recovered by Police. constable Corlett. The description reads :—Age about forty, height sft. sin., fresh complexion, dark hair, dark brown moustache, full face, brown jacket and vest, dark trousers, red flannel scarf, blue clp and shirt, blue singlet, light laced-up boots —apparently a respc :table working man. He was quite sober, and must have slipped from the dock gates, which were unprotected, owing to there being no right of way across. RUNCORN RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The fortnightly meeting of the Runcoio Rural Dis- trict Council was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present Mr. George Pilling (presiding). Rev. C. R. Nunn, Messrs. C. Roylance, H. Eyes. P. Mounfleld, G. Egerton-Warburton, J. Whitlow, A. Broome, T. Baxter, H. M. Davies, C. E. Linaker, C. E. Linker, jun., J. H. Davies, T. Wright, H. Mawdsley, S. Woodward, J. Harrison. S. Horton, C. Horton, J. Fryer, J. Spruce, J. Whitley T. Antwis, G. F. Ashton (clerk), W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), J. Swinton and W. Diggle (surveyors), J. Farrington (inspector) and Dr. Adams (medical ofli3er).—Dr. Adams reported that during the month there had been nine cases of scarlet fever, five of which were at Stockton Heath. Owing to the prevalence of scarlet fever and whooping- cough in Stockton Heath he had closed the infant schools kr a fortnight. RUNCORN HARRIERS.

Runcorn Tally Ho Harriers, having an open date on Saturday, decided to have a race between two teams selected by the Captain and sub-Captain from the mem- bers of the Club, the first six in each team to count. Although some of the senior runners were absent, 36 turned out from head quarters to go the whole course of about nine miles. The premier places in each team were easily secured by the respective captains. W. Hulse and A. Bate. Some splendid running was exhibited by the others. The surprise of the afternoon was the capital manner in whichJ. Cropper (this season's junior) chased some of the seniors home. The Sub-captain's 'team ran ont winners, as only five of the Captain's team did the distance. The teams were placed as follows : Captain's team : W. Hulse, 1 ; E. Prescott, 3 ; Cropper, 5 ; J. Sefton, 7; and C. H. Cook, 9. Sub- captain's team: A. Bate, 2; R. Lanceley, 1; W. Jones, 6 ; A. Horton, 8 ; L. Sherlock, 10, and J. Yarwood, 11.

div.head: NEW MAYOR OF WIDNES.
div.p: THE NEW MAYOR OF WIDNES.

His Worship the !Mayor (Aldermon S. Owens) took the chair at the police court on Monday, accompanied by his colleagues, Mojor Wareing. Alderman Quinn. and Mr. F. tVeil.—Mr. Peters said he would like to voice his colleagues' congratulations to him as Mayor of the borough upon taking his place on the Bench.—.lr. Knowles said he liked to see the Bench and Bar working harmoniously together, because the duties were made so much easier. The duties of the Bench were sometimes disagreeable, but he personally would try to make his position as agreeable as possible.—Mr. Poole also offered his congratulations.—The Chairman, replying, said the remarks were almost overwhelming. lie appreciated the gravity and responsibility of the office and also the warm offers of assistance from the solicitors. As far as possible he would fear God and honour the King, and mete out justice to every one, tempered with mercy.— The first case was that of Catherine Davies, aged four- teen, for stealing 721 b. weight of coal from the dock side. After a few kindly words from the Mayor the case was dismissed.

RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS. The fortnightly meeting of the Runcorn Board of Guardians was held at Dutton on Tuesday when there were present—Mr. A. R. Norman (presiding), the Rev C. R. Nunr, Messrs. C. Roylance, H. Eyes, P. Monnfield G, Egerton Warburton, J. Whitlow A. Broom,T.Baxter, H. M. Davies, C. E. Linaker, J. Ff. Davies, T. Wright. H. Mawdsley, S. Woodward, W. Harrison, George Pilling, S. Horton, C. Horton, John Fryer, J. Spruce,T., Wood, J. Whitley, C. E. Linaker, jun., T. Antwis, G. F. Ashton (clerk) W. E. Hough (assistant clerk), J. Cook, W. R. de Prez and F. Pearson (relieving officers) and J. Cunnah (master).—The Finance Committ 4c) reported payments in out-relief of £7O to Mr. Cook, £2B to Mr. de Prez and .£2B to Mr. Pearson.—Mr. Spruce reported that the number of inmates WP4 going up. There were at present 157 inmates as against 143 twelve months ago. The increase was largely in children.—The Clerk reported that the Local Govern- ment Board ha c' written that they had under considera- tion the amended plans relating to the proposed alterations and additions at the Workhouse. Attention was drawn to the suggested slight alterations in connec- tion with the mortuary and the maternity wards. Subject to these suggestions receiving the consideration of the Board, the plans would be approved.—The altera- tions were accepted and it was decided to obtain tenders for the work. RUNCORN POLICE AND PUBLICANS.

During the hearing of a licensing case at Runcorn Police Court on Monday, a lively passage occuried between Mr. A. Browne, solicitor, of Warrington, end Superintendent Ennion. The defendant was Charles Baker Pugh, who was charged with permitting drunken- ness on October 27 on his premises, the Boathouse Inn. Mersey-street. A waterman named William Marshall, of Portland-street, was accused of being drunk. Mr. Browne asked Superintendent Ennion it he was open to put a reasonable construction upon the section of the Act with regard to permitting drunkenness ?—Superin- tenpent Ennion, I am.—Here is a man comes in a house drunk, and we do not serve him. Surely, some consideration ought to be given to the publicans of Runcorn ?—Certainly, sir. Do IDo you say that when you sent a constable sneaking after a man ?—I did not send a conqable sneaking after him. I sent him to see the man safe home, because he was not in a fit state to turn into the strcsts. If a man can walk home what is wrong about him ?—lf a man is able to walk home I would be the lrst man to take steps against him. I know you are prejudiced against drink?—No, Tam not. Jam a teetotaler, but not pre- judiced. I have been a teetotaler for twenty years, and if I live another twenty years I shall not touch it. Mr. Giles (solicitor for the police).—What Mr. Browne means is, cannot you overlook a little ?—if the law is broken. I am paid to bring the offender to justice; and while lam here I shall do so. After hearing the evid- ence, the bench convicted, but said it was not a case for a heavy fine. Pugh was fined lOs and costs (£2 35.) and Marshall was fined ss. and costs.

div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
OBSTRUCTING A FOOTPATH.

Althur Richardson, James Richardson, and Thomas James were sumnioned at Newton last Thursday for obstructing a footpath by standing thereon, on Friday afternoon, at the corner of Viaduct-street and Brick- street, Earlestown.—P.C. Powell said they were jump- ing about on the footpath as well as standing on it, and obstructing foot passengers.—lnspector Innes said there had been complaints about obstruction of this kind— hence tha proceedings.—Arthur Richardson and James appeared and admitted the offence. The other Richard- son did not appear, and his brother said he had asked off but was not allowed to leave his work.—Tne Chair- man said he must come, and his case would •be adjourned, while the other two must pay 2s. 6d. includ- ing costs.

DRUNKENNESS. At Newton Petty Sessions last Thursday, Edwin Henshaw, of Haydock, pleaded guilty to a charge of drankenness, and not guilty to a further charge of assaulting the police.—P.C. Thomas said he had to get the assistanne of three other men to take the prisoner to the police station. They got him on a tramcar and it took two to hold him down there. The prisoner kicked and struck him.—The prisoner had been four times convicted (four times this year) r,d was now fined ss. for the drunkeness and 10s. for the assault on the police, and ordered to be bound over to keep the peace for six months.—The following were fined 2s. 6d. each for drunkenness : Alfred Unswortb, Hugh Cain (32 times previously con- victed, but not recently) and Eli Rumsden ; also James Wild and Frank Cnarles, of Golborne ; James Jackson and Jonathan Twist, Haydock ; Thomas Bullets and Jonathan Gleave were find ss. each and costs.

div.head: ST HELENS.
div.p: ST HELENS.
A BROKEN THIGH. EXTRAORDINARY COMPENSATION CASE.

At St. Helens County Court, on Wednesday, Richard Parsonage, labourer, of 42, Patton-street, Birkenhead, sued for an award under the Workmens's Compensation Act in respect of an accident that befel him on June 18 last on the premises of the Sutton Manor Colliery Company at Clock Face.—Mr. Newman, instructed by Mr. James Roberts, of Liverpool, represented Parson- age, who fell off a platform on the date named, and received a severe injury to the left leg and a fracture of the thigh bone. He was totally and permanently I incapacitated for work. He had worked four weeks for the company, and claimed 7s. 7d. per week. Mr. E. Peace appeared for respondents.—Parsonage gave his evidence of the accident, which happened at the Colliery Company's premises, but afterwards admitted that in 1891 he met with a serious accident at th e, Sutton Glass Works, and that he was attended in the Providence Hospital by Dr. Jackson.—Dr. Morland Hocken, of Liscard, said that on the 22nd of July he was called to see this man at Birkenhead, and he found him lying on a sofa, and his thigh was swollen and dis- coloured, and he came to the conclusion that he was suffering from a fracture of tire thigh bone. He put in an X-ray photograph which had been taken by Dr. Holland of Rodney-street, and which showed a fracture of the thigh. He claimed that this was a recent fracture. Mr. Peace called Dr. Bates, who said that he examined this man on the day of the accident, but could find no traces whatever of recent injury. He asked Parsonage if he ever hal his leg injured before, and the man replied that be had not. He found that the man had walked to his lodgings from the colliery, a distance of 500 yards, and had come dow.,stairs. He thought it was not possible for a man who had his thigh broken (as the photograph showed) to have done anything like this. When he examined the man there were no signs at all of a fracture.—Dr. Jackson said that he attended Parsonage in 1891 when he met with the accident at the Sutton Glassworks. The photograph showed the -old fracture, but the strange part was that in 1891 the man did not suffer from a fracture of the thigh.—Mr. Charles Crouch, foreman of the Sutton Glassworks, spoke to the accident and said that this man was dis- charged because he was told that the time he was drawing club money he was working at a colliery.— Judge Shand held that there had been an accident and gave an award for 7s. 7d. per week compensationr. A ST. HELENS COLLIERY FATALITY. EXTRAORDINARY INQUEST. The coroner, Mr. Brighouse, and a St. Helens jury found themselves confronted with a most remarkable and difficult question on Monday night at the inquest on William John Carter,aged twenty-nine, of 70 Morris- street, Sutton, who died in the St. Helens Hospital on Friday morning last. Mrs. Carter said that the deceased was a day wage man at the Bold Colliery, belonging to the Collins Green Company. He had always enjoyed good health, and never complained of anything. On Friday October 26th. he went to work at 5 a.m.as usual. Later she saw him in the Hospital,and he told her that he had been going down the jig brow with a full box whenfit got off the rails. He tried to get on the line again, but it overpowered him and jammed him against a prop. The day before he died he appeared to be quite well, with the exception of bruises on his hip.—Dr. Jackson said that he saw Carter soon after he was admitted to hospital. He was suffering from bruises and contusions on the left side. Witness attended him up to his death, The post-mortem revealed that one of the man's ribs was cracked on the inside. It was not fractured right through. The right side of the heart was very much distended, and the valves quite incom- petent. lire cause of death was syncope, due to the distention of the right side of the heart. He could not connect the accident 'with the death. The Coroner : Did not the injuries that he received on October 16 hasten or accelerate death ?—No. Not in any degree ?—There was no connecting link between them. He was in that condition that he might have died at any time, and under any circumstances. Any little excitement or anything happening suddenly to throw a heavy load on the heart might cause death— The Coroner said that being caught between a tub and a prop must have been somewhat exciting.—Yes, and I should have been expecting his death at that time.— Supposing that he had not received these injuries on October 26, do you think he would have died when he did ?—He might have died sooner, or he might have died later. He was in such a condition that he might have died at any time.—You won't commit yourself to the fact that the injuries hastened or accelerated death ? No.—Can you say that they did not ?—I do not know lin what way they did. There is nothing to connect the injury with the cause of death. It was getting up out of bed that caused death. After lying in bed and suddenly getting up into a chair he could not stand it, and died. —He would not have been in bed in the hospital if he had not received the injury ?—Perhaps not. —The Coroner inquired if Mr. Webster, who represented the relatives, was going to call Dr. Tough.—Mr. Webster said" No."—Dr. Jackson : Dr. Tough agrees with me. —The Coroner : You say he died from natural causes? —Yes ; the condition of the heart must have existed for a long time. The valves were enormously enlarged. One of the valves, instead of being about one inch in diameter, was several inches in diameter.—The Coroner said it was a strange thing that the fracture of the ribs had not caused death.—Witness agreed that this was so. The only explanation was that an injury did not throw a very great strain on the heart. Attempting to lift a heavy box on to the line would create a bigger strain on the heart than an injury.—Mr. Webster questioned the doctor, and suggested that the injury would lower the tone of the man's system to the extent of causing death. Dr. Jackson said he could not say that it did.—The Coroner expressed some astonishment, and said the point for the jury was whether the accident in the pit hastened the death. Although the man was crushed between the box and the prop, and.lay in hospital from October 26th to November Bth, and although he had a rib fractured, the doctor did not think that those circumstances had accelerated death.—Nurse Strachan said that the deceased was bright and apparently pro- gressing favourably. On Friday morning she assisted another nurse to lift Carter out of bed into a chair, in order that the bed might be made. Immedi- ately he got into the chair he collapsed, and death took place twenty-five minutes later.— The Coroner addressed the jury at some length, and said that the facts of the accident were admitted, In the absence of the strong evidence of Dr. Jackson he would have said that death resulted from the injury, but Dr. Jackson was very strong on the pint. He was not prepared to say that the injuries hastened death. He (the coroner) gave the relatives an opportunity of being represented at the post mortem, but it appeared that their doctor agreed with Dr. Jackson. According to him, the death was from natural causes, and it was for the jury to say if they could return a verdict to that effect. He felt, however, that they could not lose sight of the accident and the fact that the man bad .been in hospital, and he asked them to carefully consider the case.—The jury returned a verdict that death was. due to heart failure, and was accelerated by the Injuries ' received at the Bold Colliery.

div.head: WARRINGTON TRADERS AND THE SHIP CANAL. Another Petition Lodged.
div.p: WARRINGTON TRADERS AND THE SHIP CANAL. Another Petition Lodged.

In the appeal of Joseph Crosileld and Sons v. Man- chester Ship Canal Company, pending in the House of Lords, the respondents have lodged a petition asking that they may be allowed to present a cross-appeal, although their time for doing so has expired. The petition has been referred to the Appeal Committee for hearing on Monday next. It will be remembered that the gestion related to the apprehension of traders and manufacturers carrying on business near Warrington that the operations of the Manchester Ship Canal Company would have the effect of lowering the level of the water in the Alersey and cause silting in the in the portion of the river near Warrington. The Court of Appeal held on December 21, 1905, that the traders were entited to a depth of eight feet of water at Warrington, but that, by reasor‘of deposits of mud and silt in the bsd of the channel, there was a much less depth of water, and that the Canal Company were liable to put this right.
