div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
FURIOUS .NroTORING IN CHESHIRE. DRIVER FINED AT DARESBURY..

At the Da—r ;I;JY' Petty Sessions,on Tuesday, before Messrs. William Long (in the chair), H. Nield, and J. Malin Edelsten, John Henry Porter, 161, Castelnau, Barnes, Surrey (and of the firm of Boon and Porter, motor engineers, London), was charged with having on the 10th October, on the Stretton-road, Appleton,driven a motor car at a speed dangerous to the public, having regard to all the circumstances of the case. He was further charged with refusing to stop when requested to do so by the police. Superintendent Ennion stated that on October 10, at 5.43 p.m., Sergeant Kennerley was on duty on Stretton-road, Appleton, between Appleton Cross and Stretton Church, when he saw two motor cars going in the direction of Appleton Cross. Both cars were being driven at a very fast speed. The first car passed the sergeant and he stepped in front of the second car and put up his hand, and called to the driver to stop, but no notice was taken and both cars went on. The sergeant had to step out of the road. The cars came from the direction of Northwich, and were going in the direction of Warrington. The sergeant succeeded in getting the number of the car, "LC 5,746." He communicated with the police authori- ties in London, and it was ascertained that the second car belonged to a Mr. Drabble, Hyde Park, London. The defendant was the driver of the car. —Evidence in support of Superintendent Ennion's statement was given by a number of witnesses.—Thomas Broady, farmer, Appleton, said he was of opinion that the cars were racing.—Defendant said he did not think he had been fairly treated. He had received two summonses. He wrote to the police for particulars, and told them he knew nothing about the matter, and he received a letter from the Snperintendent to the effect that the facts of the case were fully stated in the sum- monses. There were, however, no particulars given on the summonses. No time was stated, and he could not find the place on the map.—The Chairman : The police officer was quite justifled in what he did. You motorists think you can ride roughshod over the country, and knock people out of your road simply to gratify your own selfish wishes to go fast.—Defendant was fined .£7 Ns. and hosts for excessive speed, and .£1 and costs for not stopping—altogether £l2 Os. 6d.

div.head: DISCUSSION AT THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS
div.p: DISCUSSION AT THE BOARD OF GUARDIANS
MEETING.

Some discussion on the case took place at the meeting of the Board of Guardians held on Wednesday under the presidency of Mr. J. Biltinge. At a meeting of the House Committee it was proposed by Mr. W. C. Brooks and seconded by Mrs. Wilkinson, that all legal proceed- ings against James Clarke be abandoned. An amend- ment was moved by Mr. A. J. Jolley and seconded by Mr. A. Brooks that Mr. Shearer should prosecute Clarke for neglecting to maintain himself. The amendment was carried by six votes to three. The Clerk submitted to the Board the correspondence with Councillor Stott which is given above. . . _

Mr. Fo2sHAw moved the confirmation of the minutes. Mr. ASHCROFT pressed for some particulars of the case to be given. Mr. FORSHA W said the man Clarke was employed, but left his employment and threw himself on the rates, and it was therefore the duty of the Guardians to prosecute him. Mr. DAVICS seconded the confirmation of the minutes.

Mr. ASHCROFT thought further particulars should be given. He was informed by other Guardians that this man was given a discharge by the Workhouse master who had no idea where he was going to. When Clarke reached the gate he was met by one of the Guardians who offered to flnd him work. The man was a free agent as the offer was made to him outside the gates. The Guardian in question, instead of going to the labour bureau where plenty of men could be obtained by paying fair wages, offered the man sd. an hour instead of Bd. or 80. Later the Guardian's son in- creased the wag& Gd. an hour and the man went on the job. Mr. BENT rose to a point of order as he contended the matter had nothing to do with the Board, Mr. KNOWLES supported Mr. Bent's protest. The matter related to a prosecution that was pending and if the discussion was not illegal it was highly improper. They were met as Guardians to discharge Board of Guardians duties. Mr. Ashcroft's speech might sound very nice delivered on a tub in the Market-place on Sunday afternoon for a lot of those peoble who did not want work, to listen to, but so far as he (Mr. Knowles) was concerned, it was neither edifying nor useful and it ' was not a patt of the business of the Board. If what had taken place was wrong, tha proper course was to , complain to the Local Government Board, and the ' House of Commons would probably sit all night to try it. (Laughter.) It would be highly improper for the Chairman of the House Committee to go into details. Mr. Foßsir.tw said that all through this case he had kept to what concerned the Guardians only, and the Board bad dealt with the matter as far as it concerned I them. Mr. Ashcroft seemed to take great pleasure in trying to drag the Guardians through the mire.

div.head: Warrington Win at Rochdale.
div.p: Warrington Win at Rochdale.

Warrington made the journey to Rochdale on Satur- day and came back with two very useful points as the result of their meeting with the Hornets. There was a capital crowd of about 4,000, and it was evident that the home club is getting much better support this season. Mr. J. H. Smith was referee and the teams lined out as follows :

Rochdale Hornets—Upton, back; Davies, Ward, Charles, and Hardman, three-quarter backs ; Baxter and Schofield, half backs ; Dearden, Turner, Richard- son, Brooks, Crabtree, and Ashton, forwards. Warrington—Berry, back ; Fish, Dickinson, Taylor, and Brooks, three-quarter backs ; Hoekenhall and Lees, half backs ; Heath, Harmer, Belton, Naylor, Shugars, and Preston, forwards. Preston commenced against the wind,and the Hornets at once rushed the ball to the line, where Warrington were penalised for obstructing Hoarder'. and Hardman landed a goal. The Hornets were still having the best of matters, and Warrington put forth a grand defence. Fine play was seen by both sides, and at length Fish got away at top speed,but Upton saved brilliantly close to the line. Harmer had a walk-over but lost the ball. Berry then charged a kick and following up had the line at his mercy, but bungled an easy chance badly. Baxter transferred play to the Warrington" 23," where Berry cleared in the nick of time. Taylor next raced away from centre and passed to Harmer, who scored. Preston improved. Half-time arrived with the score— Warrington 1 goal and 1 try (5 points), Rochdale Hornets 1 goal (2 points), The Hornets resumed with great energy, and Hardman was pulled up on the line. A dribble by Dearden was nicely marked by Hockenhall at his "23." Fish made a run down touch, and was obstructed by Upton. A free- kick was given to Warrington, bat Preston's kick wsnt wide. A rush by Warrington was saved by Hardman, who was badly injured, and had to be carried off, and after being attended to by the ambulance men, was con- veyed to the Rochdale Infirmary. From a scrummage the ball was passed along the line to Fish, who scored at the corner. Preston failed. The Hornets rallied well, and from a scrummage near the centre, Schofield broke clean away, and cross-kicked to Baxter, who robbed Brooks and scored a grand try. Davies improved. Just on time Dickenson got a try for Warrington after clever passing and re-passing with Fish, and Preston landed a goal. Result ;—Warrington 2 goals and 3 tries (13 points), Rochdale Hornets 2 goals and 1 try (7 points).

div.head: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
div.p: LANCASHIRE COMBINATION.
WARRINGTON "A" v. ROCHDALE "A."

Warrington "A " were in their happiest mood for their fixture with Rochdale "A" which attracted a large gate to the Wilderspool ground on Saturday. From the commencement of the game the issue was never in doubt. In the first few minutes Bradshaw scored and then a clever movement by Lloyd paved the way for Landor to cross. A really brilliant run by Jones ended in a third try, and Knight placed a goal from the touch line. Cartwright next crossed, to be followed by Jordan, Knight from the last try placing a goal. A forward rush ended in Jolley being awarded a try, whilst near the interval Knight, the Warrington custodian, followed up a kid, and scored, Foster plac- ing a goal. With a lead of 29 points Warrington again forced matters in he second half, and Jones, Board- man, Jordan, and Jolley scored tries, Knight aeding two goals. Rochdale scored. near time, and the final record was—Warrington, six goals eleven tries (45 points) ; Rochdale, one try (three points).

Class Teachers' Meeting. The annual meeting of the Warrington Certificated Class Teachers' Association was held on Saturday morning in the Wycliffe Memorial Buildings. There was a good attendance, presided over by Mr. F. J. Emson. Mr. S. W. Jeffrey (lion secretary) gave his report of the year's work, from which it appeared that the local branch is the third in point of numerical strength in Lancashire, practically every certificated class teacher in Warrington being .a member.—The Treasurer (Mr. T. Edden) submitted a satisfactory balance sheet, which along with the secretary's report, was adopted.—Mr. Emson called upon Mr. Arm- strong to take up the position of President of the Association for the ensuing year, and in accepting the position the new President thanked the members for the honour they had conferred upon him. Mr. Armstrong proceeded to give a brief outline of the work of the Warrington Certificated Class Teachers' AssociatiNn since its inception and of its aims and objects, in conjunction with the National Federation of Assistant Teachers' Association. The speaker also drew attention to some of the changes which had taken place in the practical working of our educational system, many of them obtained after long and arduous work through the efforts of teachers' associations, and all of them calculated to considerably lighten the burden upon the child and make his school, life healthier and happier. A strong appeal was made to the teachers of the town to heartily support and join in the work of the National Union of Teachers, and thus strengthen the hands of the Executive, so that the good work that they were doing for the cause of education, the child, and the teacher, would go on and prosper,—The following officers were appointed Vice-President, Mr. J. div.head: CAN VASES FEEL PAIN?
div.p: CAN VASES FEEL PAIN?

Whilst my daughter was playing the piano a few days ago, a glass vase containing flowers suddenly gave out a shrill noise and fell to pieces. The vase was quite sound previously, and the table on which it stood was fully two feet from the piano.—Correspondent ip "Amateur Photographer."

div.head: POLICE COURT SEQUEL. -7 Persecution Alleged.
div.p: POLICE COURT SEQUEL. -7 Persecution Alleged.

Yesterday morning Clarke was brought before the Borough magistrates and charged with wilfully neglect- ing to maintain himself whereby he became chargeable to the Union. Clarke was represented by Mr. Browne and pleaded not guilty. Mr. Shearer, who appeared to prosecute on behalf of the Board of Guardians, said that on the Bth October, Mrs. Clay telephoned to the Workhouse and said she could find work for Clarke and the man was given his dismissal. Clarke saw Mrs. Clay's son and agreed to work for him strippng the paper off the walls of some houses and shops in S ankey-street for 6d. an hour. Clarke worked 30 hours and then left, failing to return to work on the Monday following. On the 19th of October he was re-admitted to the Workhouse. The case had created great feeling in the town but he (Mr. Shearer) submitted that all he had to prove was that the defendant had work to do and wilfully refused to do it. After Clarke ceased to work for Mr. Clay, a tender was obtained for the work at ,£l6 so that had Clarke continued there was plenty of of work to keep him busy for many weeks. Mr. Awbery (master of the Workhouse) spoke to receiving the telephonic communication from Mrs. Clay and discharging Clarke. In answer to Mr. Browne witness said that whilst in the scorkhouse Clarke had been very useful and had unquestionably saved the ratepayers a large amount of money. Mr. Browne : I think that when Clarke returned he complained that he did not get enough wages ?—I cannot answer that. Did he tell you he only got 19s. 6d. during the week ? —Yes.

Dc-,-3:ou know that Clarke stripped the walls of the whole of one shop in Sankey-street and the greater part of another ?—I do not. Mr. Awbery stated that there bad been so many cases of men throwing up work and going to the Workhouse that the Board determined to prosecute in the first case.

Mr. Walter Clay said that when he showed Clarke what he had to do he asked him what wages he wanted. Clarke did not reply, and witness suggested sd. an hour. Clarke said, 'Hardly. Sly 6d.," and this price was agreed upon. Witness had occasion to complain about the small amount of work which Clarke had done and Clarke said he would throw up the job. He had not stripped one room. On Saturday Clarke drew his wages and left. Witness fully expected that he would return on the Monday, as the job was not complete, but he failed to do so. The man had never grumbled about the plj9e'„ .
Mr. Browne : Did he not ask you for more and you would not give it?—No.
Did you give him any tools ?—No. I was not aware that he had not got tools. He said he could borrow them.

Is it true that he only had an old brush which he I found on the premises ?—I do not know. Is Mrs. Clay here ?—No. I thought not. Why go to the Workhouse for labour I when there is a labour bureau in Sankey-street, and plenty of painters out of work ?—Mrs. Clay thought she was doing a good turn to the man in bringing him out of the Workhouse. Is Mrs. Clay a member of the Distress Committee ? I am sure I don't know. 6 Witness further added that he felt that Mrs. Clay had a perfect right to take a man out of the Workhouse and find him work.

Mr. Browne : At the meeting of the committee she voted for the prosecution. —lt would not be on personal grounds but because it was her duty. Is this man the only one youhave had out of .the Work- house ?—Except Hind—yes. Do you pay Hind a small rate of wages ?—I paid what was asked in both ease, .

Defendant said that when he saw Mr. Clay he wa asked to work for 5d.. but said the figure was rather too low. Mr. Clay said "It is better to receive that than be in the Workhouse," and then' offered 6d., which sum witness accepted, Mr. Clay ought to have provided the tools but did not do so. Witness stripped one shop and had almost finished the other and when Mrs. Clay com- plained that he had not done enough he replied that it would be a long time before he stripped any more rooms at the same price. He had tried to get work in Manchester but had been unable to do so. Mrs. Clay wanted him to buy his own tools and these would at least have cost him .£l. - _
Mr. Shearer : Did not Mrs. Clay arrange that she would provide you with the tools which you required.? —No, sir. She only said she would find a pair of scissors.

--Wii-e-n—you left you had not been dismissed ?—No, sir. Mr. Browne said the attitude which the Guardians took in that case was not consistent with the present- day idea of what should exist amongst the working classes, and it was thought that the Guardians had not acted rightly in allowing tho defendant to go out of the Douse, and in ordering a prosecution.in fact it is was regarded not as prosecution but as persecution at the hands of the officials and certain Guardians. It was only carried by 10 votes to six, and some of those Guardians who voted for the prosecution were Guardians who had not investigated the matter an who knew nothing about it. Were the Bench going to say that Clarke wilfully refused to work when he went to Manchester for the purpose of buying tools? The Act was never meant to cover a case like that. The Defendant in the Work- house had unquestionable done good work and saved the ratepayers a large amount of money, so that whilst he had nominally been chargeable he had done more for the ratepayers than they done for him. In the strict sense of the word he had not been chargeable. The Act was never meant to be used as a handle for spite. On moral grounds the practice of taking men out of the Workhouse ought not to be encouraged when there were plenty of unemployed painters to be had through the labour bureau.
After a brief retirement the Magistrates found Clarke guilty and sentenced him to one day's imprison ment.
er, Saturday, November 17, 1906.

div.head: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.
div.p: OUR LOCAL CHURCHES.

Wycliffe Church. The annual foreign missionary services were held at Wycliffe Church on Sunday, large congregations assembling throughout the day. The Rev. Thomas Biggin, of Pekin, China, preached in the morning and evening on mission work in China. In the afternoon he addressed the Sunday school scholars and his dis- course-was listened to with the utmost attention. The collections were in aid of the London Missionary Socieq. Wycliffe P.S.A. There was a large attendance at the Wycliffe P.S.A. Society and the proceedings were of an enthusiastic character. Mr. H. Percy Densharc, of Orford, presided, and spoke ugon " Forbearance one with another." He said the burdens of home could be lightened, by thoughtfulness and carefulness, and failure to do so brought on pain, suffering and neglect. Mr. J. Whalley. of Manchester, who is a great favourite at the meetings of the Society, referred in eulogistic terms to the lengthened services of the Rev. John Yonge, thd presi- dent. Mr. Walley founded his remarks upon the words, "Fear not; neither be dismayed." Mr. W. Rutter delighted the gathering with his cornet solo "The lost chord." Mr. W. H. Payton presided at the organ. Mr. W. Beswick and Mr. J. Hawthorn also took part in the meeting. The secretary welcomed four new members, making a total of 500. There was a good collection in aid of the funds of the Societi The Secretary returned thanks on behalf of the syidowsand family of the late ex-Inspector Rowbothai: and said they appreciated the letter of sympathy sent them by the Society in their great sorrow. He also read a letter from the Rev. J. Yonge, who could not be present, thanking the brethren for their letter of congratulation to him on completing his 30 years' service at Wycliffe Church as their pastor.

Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church. Preaching at Bewsey-road Wesleyan Church on Sunday evening the Rev. S. Pitt took for his subjeet : "Boldness." Few qualities, he said, were more to be desired in the church to-day than the Divine quality of boldness. Amongst all things which Ivid lessened the hold on the people of the Church of Christ perhaps not the lease was that the visible Church had so often been wanting in the courage of her convictions and her creed How slow the Church had been in taking her stand as to the desolating traffic in intoxicating drink. Great pro- gress had been made in their own church in recent years. They had no need to blush for Methodism in that matter. He wished they could say the same all round but the most damaging charge which could be made against the great historic Church of England was the fatal complicity in which she stood with thiat growing evil. The Bishops who were carving the Edncation Bill in the name of religion swallowed the Licensing Bill, bolus bolus,and their talk of religion now suffered a tremendous discount. In other matters ' the Church was wanting in boldness such as the unscru- pulous accumulation of wealth. They must say some- thing about that and that something must be of a nature which would sting.—The preacher at the morning service was Mr. R. J. Moss.

Holy Trinity Church. Sunday next will witness the re-opening of the organ at Holy Trinity Church which has undergone consider- able renovation. The regular worshippers at this church will have noted the great improvements which have been effected in the interioy of the buildings Within the last eighteen months the whole of the light- ing has been renewed, and decorations carried out ; while recently a new baptistery has been placed in the west end in memory of the late Miss Garven. In order to complete the cycle of improvements it has long been felt that the organ needed a thorough renovation. Originally it stood in the west gallery, and portions of it are probably almost as old as the church itself. Some thirty years ago it was taken down and rebuilt in its present position, with modern additions. Since then little appears to have been done to it beyond the periodical tunings which have of late years been accomplished with increasing difficulty and with damage to the pipes. After mature consideration, it was decided to have the an renovated, and has been corn pletely dismantled; every pipe and every part o the mechanism being overhauled, cleaned, and, wher- necessary, renewed.- The total cost of the work is ZlOO

- DEAR CHILDREN, , I suppose there are some of my nieces and nephews who have heard of that old Latin saying, "Tempus Fugit," which means "Time flies." Well, to me this week has been Tempus fugitting with a vengeance; it only seems but yesterday since I sat down to write last week's letter, then, as the clown says, "Here we are again." I hope you are all trying for those three Christmas prizes, for the best new things suitable for the Christmas party. I have not received many contributions yet. I hope a lot of you are not refraining because you believe your jokes, tale, game, or some- thing, stands no chance. / Why, it may be you's which will get the ffrst prize. Have any of you tried the "Good morning Madam to Eve. said Adam" on your friends? If so write and tell me how you succeeded with it. I don't know whether any of you have heard that little tit- bit about the tramp watching a farmer in a field, and asking him this question, "I don't ouppcse as yer don't want nobody to do nothing for yer, don't you?" and the farmer looks up, at him and answers .curtly, "Yes, I don't." By the way who says a free bottle of Mason's delicious " Extract c.f Herbs"? One of my little nephews has just written for a bottle, and it reminds me I have a dozen or so still left which I am anxious to present to you. Well,. I have no more to tell you) this week beyond the fact that the League welcomes seven fresh members, several of whom have fur- nished me with "nice, interesting little pieces. Be good, my dear children, and don't forget the address of UNCLE. NED.
WELCOME TO Susannah Parkinson. Emily Woolliams. Agnes Nicholas. Amy Deeming. Margaret Constance Knight. Helena Doris Knight.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l should like to be one of your nieces, and I am sending you a piece of poetry, which I hope you will like.

From ycnir foving niece, SUSANNAH PARKINSON. BABY'S SLEEP. Creeping so softly over the floor, Now here by the window, now there by the door; Herself pulling up, by chair and by bed, Getting many a bump on her dear little head, Little sharp eyes, spying every stray pin, Little mouth open to put them all in. Laughing and crowing with frolicsome glee, As merry a child as you'll anywhere see— Our dear little wide-awake baby. A little warm thing, cuddled down in a heap, Her soft cheeks aflush with the roses of sleep; Little smiles hidden all safely away, To be brought forth again at the dawn of Clay. Little feet resting, and little hands, too, Which is more than by daylight they ever can do; Tucked in with many a kiss and caress, May angels watch o'er her, may God ever bless— Our dear little sound-asleep baby.
ISN'T IT MOTHER?

When buttons come off and clothes are worn,,' If accidents happen and rents are torn, Holes in our s4sckings and holes in our socks, Places to mend in our jackets and frocks, Whom do we find is our truest friend? Isn't it mother who's ready to mend? If things all go wrong, and we've heavy hearts, Squabbles and tumbles, bruises and smarts, If fingers are cut or scratched or burnt, If lessons are hard and won't be learnt, Whenever there's trouble, whenever there's pain Isn't it mother we come to again? If sickness should lay us low on our bed, With weary limbs and an aching head; When fever renders us helpless and weak, And steals the colour away from our cheek; When suffering comes as it sometimes will, Isn't it mother we look to still? When sunshine enfolds our lives with light, And everything goes smooth and bright; , If pleasures abound, and sweet success Fills us with radiant happiness; When blessings are poured on her girl or boy, Isn't it mother who's full of joy? ANNIE V. CALLING.

Dear I:incle Ned,—l am only seven years old, but I should like to be one of your little nieces. I am going to make something for your poor tittle ones to keep them warm in the cold feather, and mother is going to help me. I lave written :this all by myself. With love and big Kiss (X), I an, your new little niece, HELENA DORIS KNIGHT.

Dear Uncle Ned, —I hardly know how td thank you for the beautiful box of chocolates which I received all safe. It is very kind of you, and I am pleased to think that I won the second prize. I hope that you will like my story, which is original, and that I shall, see it in print. I remain, your loving niece, ELSIE LEWIS.

PRINCESS DISCONTENT. Once upon a time, there lived in a beautiful country, a King and Queen, whose names were Grelda and Halms., and they had a little girl, whose real name was Nesta, but she never was pleased with, anything and was always so dis- agreeable that the people called her "Dis- content." As she grew older she beCarna so selfish and unbearable that King Grclda offered a handsome reward to any one who could cure his daughter of her selfishness. Princess Discontent was really a pretty girl, but she had an evil disposition, and her mouth drooped ,at the corners. One beautiful evening Princess Discontent was having a large Party, to celebrate her fourteenth birthday; she had grumbled at everything she had come across, and when all her little guests were dancing, she slipped out of the palace and into the gar, den without being noticed. She sat down under a fir tree, where she began to sob bitterly. "Oh, dear," she cried, "nobody likes me, my life is a perfect misery." "Oh, you wicked, ungrateful girl," said a little voice close beside her, and on looking round she saw a little old woman with a red cloak. i Then the little woman went on: "Your father and mother have tried their best to please you, and yet you grumble and snarl, but now your punishment has come, for you will go with me to a land of Peace and Brightness, to see if, at the end of -three years, you can' be restored to your parents, a happy, eOntented girl." Then, all of a sudden, Princess Discontent found herself in a lovely garden, where pretty little -girls were splashing about in 'a marble fountain. Then a group/of happy little girls came to meet her. he was just going to say, "Go away, what do you want?" when' they threw their/arms about her and said: "Come and have a game with us, dear Nests." Princess Discontent actually ran away with them, laughing. When Princess Discontent was missed, the Kin',' offered large -rewards to any- one who could find her, but of course they 'couldn't. Well, Princess Discontent was getting on splendidly in the Land of Brightness; she was learning to be happy and kind. One day she fell asleep, and the little old woman came to her and said: "Princess Nesta, you may now go to your home and to your parent's who are mourning you for dead, for you have learnt to be happy and sweet, and, above all, to be contented." Then Princess Nesta awoke, to find herself in her father's garden. She rushed into the palace and flung herself into her father's arms, saying 2 "Father, I have come back to you a better girl, and I have' learnt the lesson of contentment." The King and Queen were delighted, and she was such a happy, rind girl that the people called her no longer Princess Discontent, but "Our dear Princess Content." ELSIE LEWIS.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l saw recently the "Children's Corner," and was pleased to see that I had obtained a box of chocolates through that delightful piece of poetry, "When Daddy was a boy." I have not, however, received them, and this is why I write to you. I thought, perhaps you had forgotten them or they had been mislaid by post. I further ask for the rules, mentioned in the last issue, of the society., Please send them as soon as possible. With alb good wishes,

I remain, youc. loving nephew, GEORGE KIRS. [I am sorry, George, to cause you anxiety about the box of chocolates you were fortu- nate enough to win, but the reason of the delay was (I blush to own it) Uncle Ned's carelessness in mislaying your address. I expect by now you know how toothsome they are.]

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am sorry that I did not write before, and I am afield you will think I am not a very industrious member, but am sorry sorry I have forgotten you. Please may X have a bottle of Extract of Herbe?' Yours truly, NELMS, BEAWORTH.

[Yes, Nellie, I began to think you had left ut and gone to America or some other distance-,, but am glad to hear you are still with M. Perhaps you will send me in something for my Christmas column, in _return for the nice bottle of Extract of Herbs I am sending you.]

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am writing to thank you for the beautiful book you have sent me. lam very pleased with it, and consider it well wortii trying to win. I am sorry I could not write. sooner, but I have had no time. With all good wishes, From your loving nephew, Arammn.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l should like very much to be one of your nieces. I am nine years old. I am going to make something for one of your "poor little ones." My two sisters and I work for the "Waifs and Strays Socie4," So mother says we ought to send you something too With love, I am, Your new little niece, MARGARET CONSTANCE KNIGHT..

JAMES DODDS. Nov. 15th, 190 G. _ A Plea for Liberal Unity. Sir,—As an elector in the Latchford Ward, permit me to offer a few remarks about Mr. Parker's letter. Sir,—There appears to be so much unreap amongst He says there has been a total absence of humour in the the Liberals of ‘Varrington in consequence of the differ- controversy. lam inclined to agree with him there. ences of opinion created by the Non-Trading agitation But why didn't he write sooner? Mr. Parker's peculiar that it may not be inopportune for me to express a style of humour belongs to the unconscious variety. desire for peace andunity. The great national interests To appreciate and enjoy it thoroughly, you want a which, as far as Warrington is concerned, the Liberal reprint of the proceedings of the Inquiry into Corpora- party hold in trust, are of too great importance to allow tion Trading, a few of the handbills issued during the the differences in regard to the policy in municipal elections, a report of the last meeting of the Council, affairs to endanger the peace and well-being of the and a copy of the ten commandments. With these party. Let all concerned know by this, that as far as before you, and a little patience, the smile is bound to the leaders of the party are concerned they will not come. Mr. Parker's letter gives one the impression countenance attempts to thrust out of the party any of that whilst he was writing it he stopped several times its loyal members. I ask every true Liberal to set his to consider which side he was on. Like Balaam of old and her face against the spirit of dissention engendered he did not seem to know whether he was going to curse by differences of opinion on municipal government, and or to bless. But eventually he had to say something not to allow such to weaken and endanger the cohesion definite and he decided that he would have voted for of the patty. Now is the time when every sensible Mr. Wilson. The President of the Warrington Liberal Liberal should try and extend the spirit of toleration Association would have voted for the Tory candidate, and good feeling, and while accenting the differences whilst the other candidate was a well-known Liberal,an , which exist on a minor issue, join in a strenuous effort honoured and respected townsman, and in every respect ' to hold high the principles of reform,which have in the la suitable candidate. Let us bear this in mind for I past made the party the rallying point of all who desire future reference. He would not have voted on political national progress. Let us banish that spirit of narrow- I grounds, of course. Modern politics have nothing to ness which like a canker worm threatens to destroy the do with consistency. He would have voted for unity which is essential to success. " interest " against "principle." If I have in the past by my endeavours in any way Let us deal with another phase of Mr. Parker's gained the confidence of the party, let it be now shown, humour. He says that Non-Traders should be governed not alone in loyalty to myself, but in loyality to the Iby the rule that in things doubtful there should be party which only can be strong if supported by all I liberty, and in all things there should be charity. Let lovers of progress and freedom. Yours etc. us examine first how the two political organizations CHARLES E. PARKER. were governed by this rule. It was doubtful how many (President of the Warrington Liberal Association.) Tories in Latchford Ward agreed with the Non-Traders Penketh, Nov. 14, 1906. about municipal affairs, so why did the Tory Executive Committee leave party lines and attack Non-Traders quite early in the contest,by a reference in their circular as follows :—" Councillor Wilson is opposed by the leader of the Non-Trading Party, whose followers have pursued a course of action in the Council which is opposed to all the best and dignified traditions of public life." It will be observed that they were careful not to say anything definite. It was simply nonsense and they know it was. They evidently thought that any kind of stuff would do for Latchford. I wonder what a " dignified tradition " is like. In all my literary researches I have never met with one. I will enquire at the Library. To return to Mr. Parker's rule,why did the Tory Executive not leave their followers at liberty to use their own judgment about Non-Traders ? The same remarks apply substantially to the Liberal organization. In things doubtful the Liberals of Latch- ford Ward were not given their liberty. They were influenced by misleading handbills in which politics were quite forgotten. Let us test Mr. Parker's rule now with reference to the Non-Trading agitation and the Inquiry. We will leave out for the present the words immoral or illegal trading, because even in a court of law, when all parties concerned can be compelled to give evidence, it is very difficult to determine the nature of many business trans- actions. How then was it possible to complete the inquiry at Warrington when many traders, either ignored the Inquiry, or declined to give evidence. To apply Mr. Parker's rule, they probably thought some of the transactions were of a doubtful character, and they took the libeity of refusing information. But the inquiry went far enough to show conclusively that in connection with the town's business, and the trading between the Corporation and companies of all kinds a most irregularand unsktisfactory state of things existed, a state of things which was detrimental to the interests of the general body of ratepayers. Is Mr. Parker pre- pared to dispute that statement ? Assuming that Mr. Parker has read all the evidence which was given at the inquiry and considered all the points which were raised in the correspondence will he now say that the agitation was unnecessary, that nothing unusual or exceptional was discovered? Does he think a similar state of things exists in a majority of the boroughs in England? If he can get any reliable evidence to that effect it will do more than anything else to restore peace because if an evil is general and widespread it can only be suitably remedied by the Legislature. "In all things doubtful there should be liberty." No, it is a rule which will not stand much scrutiny, but if Mr. Parker is prepared to carry it out to its logical con- clusion, let him write to the Council and say, "It is doubtful in my opinion whether there is anything wrong about these things which the Non-Traders have been agitating about, so I think everyone should be at liberty to go on as before." One word in conclusion about charity. The rates I believe are not paid for charitable purposes and the Coun- cillors have no right to be charitable with other people's money. But it will be said : Mr. Parker means that councillors and others should have charitable feeling; towards each other. I agree with that, but I did not see anything of a charitable nature on the election handbills about the Non-Traders, neither is there any indication of charitable feelings in the report of the last Council meeting. One of the Alderman after trying to fit a teetotal cap on the heads of two Non-Traders apparently without the slightest justification used language which could not be reported. The Mayor's plea for unity and concord was forgotten in about an hour I think. This was a specimen of what the Tories call "the best and dignified traditions of public life."—Yours &c.,

Mr. C. E. Parker and Latchford Election. Sir,—Unlike a document which helped to paint Latchford red a fortnight ago, Mr. Parker's letter in your last issue was obviously the product of the man whose signature it bore. I have heard him talk in the same dreary way at public meetings, and have been as thankful when he sat down as I was to get to the end of his lengthy but not very luminous letter. His opinion on the action of a Liberal Ward Com- mittee fighting tooth and nail to return a Tory candi- date, the public would have been interested to hear, but he evaded the point. The very superior—not to say patronizing—tone he adopts may be an incurable de fect,but he ought to realize that it is not likely to help forward the peace he pro- fesses to desire. If he happened to be in league with some of the old "Traders," and had undertaken on their behalf to sit ponderously upon the Non-Traders I without committing himself to anything in particular, his letter would have been admirably suited to the purpose, and coupling this view with the action of some Liberal wire-pullers in the Latchford election, one , wonders how long it will be before the Liberal rank and Me realize that their interests are very secondary in the mind of some of their leaders. Every November the evidence becomes stronger that these leaders will sacrifice both party and principle to give the Non-Traders a fall,and the subterfuges adopted to keep the electors quiet cannot continue to serve this purpose for ever. Many have had their eyes opened, and the light is growing. Is Mr. Parker putting his money on‘ the wrong horse? The 'race may seem a foregone conclu- sion to him, but if he is wise he will "have a bit the other way " in case his friends in the trading camp don't pull off the final after all.—Yours LIBRA. Warrington, November 16th, 1906.

Sir,—ln ray letter in your issue of the 3rd I said that if the Liberal Chairman and party would follow a course suggested to my mind by a letter from Mr. W. Peter Rylands, the occupation of the Non-Traders would be gone. For five years past I have led the strenuous fight for the stoppage of what is now known in Warrington as immoral trading, that is trading through limited com- panies with the Corporation, which though legal is morally just as reprehensible and demoralising as trading through private firms or as individuals which is illegal. During that long struggle I have not said or written a single thing which has been successfully challenged, if challenged at all. The Liberal President might have concluded therefore, that when I mentioned the Liberal Chairman,l meant the Liberal Chairman,and not the Liberal President. I named the Liberal Chairman because at the beginning of the agitation it was the Liberal Chairman (Councillor Tinnion) who in the Council Chamber on January 7th, 1902, stated the Liberal view in regard to ' immoral trading. He said that" so long as such trading was within the law it should not be called into ques- tion." The then Conservative leader in the Council (Alderman Sutton) endorsed this viewat the same meet- ing, adding that "so long as the law allowed certain members of the Council who were also members of limited Companies to enter into contracts with the Cor- poration the Council had 110 right to interfere with I them. f the Non-Traders wanted to stop legal trading they must go to the Houses of Parliament, and ask them to alter the law." The Non-Traders did nothing of the kind suggested by the party leaders, but at great personal expense they held great meetings, they used the press, and they contested elections, and ulti- mately so touched the consciences of the rank and file of both political parties that company trading, or immoral trading, as it is now called,was discredited and stopped. The Conservative Chairman to-day frankly admits that the objection of the Non-Traders was rightly taken in the past. I have been and am curious to know whether to-day's Liberal Chairman (Councillor James Evans) still stands where stood the Liberal Chairman of five years ago, or whether like the Conservative Chairman, he now approves of the main plank of the Non-Trading platform, the stoppage of the startling an& expanding amount of immoral trading in vogue in Warrington five or six years ago and which the Non-Traders then challenged and have so successfully overthrown. For some unknown reason the Liberal chairmara sits tight, but the Liberal president comes along to take his place. Mr. C. E. Parker has stepped in where Coun- cillor Evans has not ventured to tread. His reply to my invitation that the Liberal chairman should,on behalf of his party, accept the views expressed by Mr. W. Peter Rylands, and so adopt an attitude of hostility to illegal and immoral trading by members of the Council with the Corporation, is strangely paradoxical, and its meaning is accordingly obscure. He says it is surely scarcely necessary for him to endorse this view, either personally or as representing the Liberal party. That may mean that he is so clearly with us that we need have no further anxiety regarding him, as it may mean that we know him to be so unalterably opposed to us that had we addressed him we should have been wasting our time and energy in so doing. His declara- tion is a double-edged deliverance that may be applied either way according to the needs of the moment. 'Sam Weller" told some admiring female listeners that he hoped Messrs. Dodson and Fogg would get the reward they deserved for their kindness, but the kind of reward be meant differed widely from the kind of reward they thought he meant when they applauded the sentiment ! But Mr. C. E. Parker goes on to to say that he and his party approve the moral teaching of the Ten Commandments, and that would appear to imply that Mr. Parker is endeavouring to show that what he really means is that he is a convert—a very tardy one it is true but still a convert, to the party which has laid down the fundamental rule that no public man shall use his public position for his private ends. But, again, Mr. Parker is sorely disappointing ! He is opposed to immoralities, but wants morality defined, and, though fail to see that he has found an infallible standard, he shews us what his ideas of public morality would be ! He would not grudge (Ist) the legitimate payment of any Councillor who undertakes special work for the Council ; (2nd) he would be bound in justice to acknowledge such a claim " if all the members of the Council demanded " reasonable payment for ordinary services," and (3rd) he would have voted for Councillor Wilson, if he had had a vote in Latchford, in vindica- tion of his belief in " the morality of adequate payment for services rendered." This is indeed public morality of the first water ! The first two of the above three suggestions are in favour of what are to-day absolute illegalities, and contrary to all accepted ideas of sound public policy,and the second(the payment of members of Councils) has been responsible for the most humiliating immoralities known to representative government. "Spoils for the victors" is a rare incentive to morality! and parity, to say nothing of the upholding of the Ten Commandments, as Tammany has so frequently shown ns. The third suggestion, the payment of Mr. Wilson is, as I have been advised by the first legal expert on such matters, illegal, though, as a preliminary, I adopted the milder method of fighting the question before the electorate on the moral issue. It may be however, that I am taking Mr. Parker too ,• seriously. He complains that in this controversy therel has been a total absence of humour; perhaps by hisl letter to you last week he is trying to remedy that; • Total. Male. Female • defect. If so we can only thank hire for his efforts to; Births Legitimate 35 17 18 amuse ;if we accept his humour, however, he must ~ Illegitimate 1 1 excuse us if we find his ideas of public morality ! div.head: W. MIMES.
div.p: W. MIMES.

Non-Traders and the Political Leaders. Sir,—lt seems to me that the principles finally in dispute in the recent New York election bear a strange 'similarity to, and in some respects are upon all fours I with, the position of affairs in our own town as between the Traders and Non-Traders. Mr. Hearst's great relative success was largely obtained through his declaration in favour of "purity in politics " without which he said in America or elsewhere, the public ownership of public utilities would be a great menace to the public weal. This is precisely what the Non• Traders say with regard to Warrington. They say that if the Corporation Works and business are carried on for the private advantage of the members, the ratepayers must and will suffer, and that but for their past and present action the rates would now be something like 10s. in the £, and consequently all rest progress and prosperity in the Town would stop—Surely a fight in such a cause must be a good one, and it cannot be either a personal or selfish one, as whatever benefits are obtainable, are equally shared by all the ratepayers. In your correspondence columns I see letters from Mr. James Dodds and Mr. Charles E. Parker. It is all very nice for the latter to express a willingness to speak a word of peace, but surely he can understand that when men of the character of Mr. Dodds are fighting for what they believe to be a good and necessary principle of public purity, they cannot allow what appears to them to be an open and flagrant breach, to pass unchallenged. That is the sum and substance of the Latchford opposition to Mr. Wilson. And again lam forcibly reminded, in the curious composition of the forces working tooth and nail for Mr. Wilson, of the New York Election referred to. Surely such a combina- tion was never seen in harness together before. What satisfaction either Mr. Parker or Mr. Rylands, as politicians, can see or obtain from results of such con- tests it is very difficult to understand. In fact the only persons interested, to benefit or suffer, are the rate- I parrs—unless indeed both political parties sustain injury by the discouraging and alienating of their own true political supporters, for the time they want them by dragging the voters out in these municipal contests and asking them to vote in a way they don't feel inclined to do. And I should like to know in a Non- Trading contest what arnonnt of influence either chair- man possesses. Beyond the assistance of what portion of their respective political machinery is willing to work, I doubt that they have any further advantage. I quite agree that it is desirable that the occupation of the Non-Traders should be gone, and when this fortunate time arrives I am sure they will be only too happy to convert their spears into pruning hooks. The question is, has it arrived yet ? If not, I would respect- fully suggest to Messrs. Rylands and Parker, as politicians, not to interfere with the ratepayers in their election of councillors.

I know very little about the Liberal party, but lam confident that when a parliamentary election arrives, if Mr. Rylands will reserve his strength and the favour of his party and get Sir Gilbert Greenall to drive him round in the yellow carriage, that the old Tory love and enthusiasm will break out as strong as ever it did in the old days when I was actively concerned for the cause, and that the result will be satisfactory for the one at the time put up at the front carryiny "Blue."— Yours truly, H. J. LONGTON.

div.head: Exarainer, Saturday, November 17, 1906.
div.p: The Exarainer, Saturday, November 17, 1906.
MR. DODDS AND MR. W. P. RYLANDS.
CORRESPONDENCE ON THE LATCHFORD ELECTION.
Conservative Chairman Supports the Non- Trading Principle.

Penketh House, Near Warrington, 3rd November, 1006. William Peter Rylands, Esq., Chairman Warrington Conservative Association. Dear Sir,—l have to call your attention to a state- ment you made at the Conservative Club after the declaration of the poll on Thursday night, namely that "just because Councillor Wilson had taken a certain office to which it was well known and understood there was a small emolument attached, and Councillor Wilson acted exactly as other Mayor's Auditors had done in taking that small remuneration, he was vituperated by the Non-Trading party in a manner which was abso- lutely scandalous.' Had this assertion not been made by you as Con- servative Chairman, I should not have troubled to notico it, but as it was I have no alternative. You knew, or you ought to have known, when you made the statement, that on November Ist, 1902, the Non-Traders first entered the Council ; that on that day they defeated the then Mayor's Anditor, and that from that time no Mayor's Auditor has received ant, fee until a few weeks ago, when for the year to March 1906, Mr. Wilson accepted £3O. This rendered it impossible for the Non-Traders, without deserting and dishonouring the main principle of their movement, to refrain from bringing the issue before Mr. Wilson's constituents and challenging his re-election. A candidate was secured ; his health failed at the last moment, two Conservatives were unsuccessfully approached. I only consented to stand because no one else could be got in time. That, however, by the way. What I take entire excep- tion to is your assertion that Mr. Wilson " was vituperated by the Non-Trading party in a manner which was absolutely scandalous." I must ask you for proof of this serious charge. I have gone over my speeches and addresses and the two short speeches of Mr. Councillor Pemberton (and no one else of the Non- Traders has publicly referred to the subject) and I assert that beyond a most fair and absolutely necessary statement of the facts, and an explanation of the public grounds of our opposition to Mr. Wilson's re-election, not a word of personal or improper censure of Mr. Wilson has been uttered by any Non-Trader. In my address in order to be as moderate as possible I omitted to use the word " immoral " (which would have been the accurate one in the circumstances though in no offensive sense) and substituted the words " highly improper," and I distinctly stated in both my speeches that I had nothing but the kindliest feeling towards Mr. Wilson personally. Mr. Wilson very frankly , stated to me in the polling booth that he realised this, I and that he recognised that 1 was fighting solely for the underlying platform of the Non-trading party, and at the declaration of the polls be also most fully and frankly thankeid me for the very friendly way in which I had concluctbd the contest throughout. Under these circumstances I have no alternative but to insist upon your giving me chaper and verse for your unjust and entirely uncalled-for charge that Mr. Wilson was vituperated by the Non-Trading party in a manner that was absolutely scandulous." or upon your withdrawing and apologising for a most wanton and a most ungenerous attack upon Councillor Pemberton and myself, and upon the Non-Trading party. I reserve the right to publish this letter together with your reply which I now await and I am,

div.head: (signed) JAMES DOODS, Chairman, Warrington Non-Trading Association.
div.p: (signed) JAMES DOODS, Chairman, Warrington Non-Trading Association.

Dingle Bank, Lymm, 12th November, 1006. Dear Sir,—l regret that absence from home has pre- vented me from replying earlier to your letter. While Ido not admit your right to "insist" upon an explana- tion of the words to which you refer, words employed in the heat of the election time, I still think they not unfairly represented the impression formed by readers of speeches made in opposition to Councillor Wilson. The whole point of that election turned upon Coun- cillor Wilson's personal conduct in accepting a fee for work done as Mayor's Auditor, and that conduct was undoubtedly characterised as immoral, improper, and illegal, and those suggestions with variations running through all the speeches of his opponents were, in my opinion, unquestionably calculated to convey the impression of a most serious imputation upon Coun- cillor Wilson's personal honour. lam pleased to note that this was not intended and with that expression of opinion on your part which I readily accept, that phase at all events of the controvery, may now be considered at rest. As regards Councillor Wilson's action this appears not only to have been not illegal, but I understand actually and specifically sanctioned by Act of Parlia- ment, and consequently cannot be deemed to be "trading" of a character to be condemned. At th same time, the Conservative Party as "Non-Traders" in the broadest sense will, I am convinced, be with me in expressing the opinion that it would be better that no payments should be made to any member of the Cor- poration for work done for the Corporation or by the Corporation, and if possible it would be desirable that the Mayor's Auditor should be selected from outside the ranks of the Corporation, in which case payment for his services, no doubt well entitled to pecuniary recognition, could be made without question or com- plaint. The point however is not one of first class importance, and cannot be compared with the broad principles of " Trading " to which objection has been rightly taken in the past. With this expression of opinion I must ask you to excuse me from pursuing further a controversy which has already been the subject of so much correspondence in the local papers during the past few weeks.—Yours faithfully, (Signed) W. PETER RYLANDS. J. Dodds, Esq.

Penketh House, Near Warringten, Nov. 15th, 1906. Dear Sir,—l have your letter of the 12th instant. Unfortunately for your defence, I find that the first word you condemn in your letter, namely "immoral," was not once used by any Non-Trader in regard to, Councillor Wilson's personal conduct, and that the words" improper " and " were solely used by me. I was careful to say" improper as I believed," and illegal as I was advised," and I cannot see by what milder or more courteous terms I could have stated the case against Councillor Wilson. Your charge was that Councillor Wilson was vituper- ated 411 y the Non-Traders in a manner absolutely scanda-" ions. Clearly you have had no ground for this, nor for your charge that it was difficult to avoid the "suspicion that the Non-Trading party is a political organization working directly against the Conservative cause," nor for your further statement that Councillor Wilson "acted exactly as other Mayor's auditors had done," the facts being that the Non-Traders have been absolutely neutral in politics,and that since the bad old days before the Non-Traders' advent into the Council in 1902, no Mayor's auditor had been paid one penny until Councillor Wilson accepted .C3O this year. "In the heat of election time " allowances are claimed. I have claimed none myself, although I have been in the van of the purity fight for 5 years past, during which time I have so written and spoken that not a single statement I have made has been so far I successfully challenged, if challenged at all. With such a record I cannot allow you or any one else to include me in an unfounded charge of" vituperation"— "scandalous "or otherwise. Nor indeed can I allow to pass your suggestion that in my last letter I expressed an opinion that no imputation upon Coun- cillor Wilson was intended. What I said and what I repeat is that nothing in the slightest degree uncalled for was uttered concerning Councillor Wilson. Your concluding remarks I have perused with great satisfaction. lam glad you approve of the objection , the Non-Traders have taken to "trading "in the past, and that you are against payment to members of the Corporation for work done for or by the Corporation, and that you think it would be desirable that the Mayor's Auditor should be selected from outside the Corporation. Unfortunately, as the law stands the Mayor's Auditor must be a member of the Council ; on the other hand, the Municipal Corporations Act 1882 distinctly provides that no member of a Council should under any pretext receive any profit or payment in respect of his membership of a Council. I have had the opinion of the foremost expert lawyer on such matters and he advises the payment is " illegal."—l am, &c., (Signesl) JAMES DODDS. [W. Peter Rylands, Esq., Chairman Warrington Conservative Association.]

div.head: ' MR. HAVELOCK WILSON'S AFFAIRS.
div.p: ' MR. HAVELOCK WILSON'S AFFAIRS.
Ten Shillings in the Pound Offered.

At the adjourned first meeting on Thursday of the creditors of Mr. J. Havelock Wilson, M.P., for Middles- borough, and president of the Sailors and Firemen's Union, a vote was taken upon the debtor's offer of a composition of 10s. in the pound, ani the Official Receiver declared the proposal had not been accepted by the necessary majority. He added that as the state- ment of affairs showed liabilities £3,383, and no assets whatever, the proposal was obviously beneficial to the creditors. The reason of the non-acceptance was that several creditors who had lodged proofs had neither sent voting letters not taken the trouble to attend the meeting, and they consequently had to be taken as voting against the proposal. The debtor asked for an adjournment on the ground that practically all the creditors were in favour of the arrangement, and by general consent the meeting was further adjourned for a week.

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND ATHLETICS.
RUGBY FOOTBALL.
[By " Ovalist."]

Granted a fine day ther e should be a big attendance on the Warrington ground this afternoon for the semi-final of the Lancashire Cup. Warrington have been very fortunate in having been drawn at home in each round and there is little daubt locally that they will add another victory to their record at Oldham's expense to-day. A great deal will depend on the work of the home forwards, and lam hoping to see them reproduce their best form in this encounter. Of late they have been under a cloud and a big effort will be necessary to get the better of the Oldham vanguard. Special training has been indulged in this week, and the men are keen on qualifying for the final tie. Once there, they are confident that they can beat either Runcorn or Broughton Rangers on neutral ground.

Though Isherwood has got his arm out of the sling and has been practising this week, it would not have been wise to play him in so important an encounter. Dickenson therefore retains his place at left centre. The backs will, in fact, be the same as last week and should be quite equal to the Oldham combination, which has not the reputation it once had. Warrington's biggest and best forwards are all available for the encounter.

The team is : —Berry, full back ; 1 ish, Dickenson Taylor and Brooks, threequarters ; Lees and Hocken- hall, half-back ; Preston, Boardman, Thomas, Naylor, Heath, and Harraer, forwards. Oldham team has been selected as follows : Thomas, full back ; Oldersbaw, Dixon, Tyson, and Cash, threequarters ; A. Lees and White, half-backs; Ferguson, Smith, Avery, Vowles, Topham and Owens, forwards.
-- The respective records of the two semi-finalists in the Lancaliire Cup Competition are as follows :
- - G. T. P. G. T. P. Warrington Warrington
G. T. P. G. T. P. Oldham 4 3 17 St. Helens 1 4 14 Oldham 4 4 20 Rochdale

A new half-back will turn out to-day for the " A ' team against Widnes Rangers. Not much informa- tion can be gleaned officially, but his name is given as Wilson, of "the South of England." lam informed that he is a half-back with a good reputation. A new local forward, Holbrook is also having a trial in this match. Team :—Knight, full back; Jordan, Jones, Cartwright and Landor, three-quarters; J. Davies and Wilson, half-backs; Swift, Belton, P. Boardman, Holbrook, Forster and Jolley, forwards.

Warrington did not dare to lose at Rochdale, or it is probable that they would have done so. They have been so criticized for not having won at Salford and 1 Broughton, that they had to beat the Hornets, and beat them they did by the respectable score of 13 points to 7 points. There was not this much differ- ence between the teams on the general run of the play, for the home lot were surprisingly vigorous and I persistent, and a less sound defence that Warrington's would have fallen more than once. It was a capital game and the Hornets' supporters, who assembled in stronger force than for years past, were well pleased witti the display of the losers. For most of the second half they were a man short, but as is often the case, they played even better football than before. War- rington's superiority was in the backs, whose straight running and passing in the later stages of the game proved too good for the Hornets. Much of the first half was spent in punting by both sides, Warrington once more following a bad example. The Hornets dashed away and scored almost in the first minute, a penalty goal being given against War- rington for some not very obvious offence. Play was very -vigorous, and Warrington several times looked like getting the upper hand. Once, Harmer charged the full back's kick and got the ball only to drop it when he had a clear course to the line. Then Berry did almost the same thing when he had even a better chance of opening his scoring account. He dribbled the ball to near the line, and then tried to pick up but was so slow about it that the Hornets got up and pre- vented a score. Eventually Taylor bluffed the home centres at half-way by pretending to kick and then racing for the line. He cleared everybody and passed to Harmer on the line, for this ever-active forward to score under the posts. Preston added a goal and gave Warrington a useful lead, which they maintained to the interval.

The Hornets re-started without Charles at centre, but a fine run by Ward gave Warrington a fright, and the attack was only checked on the line. Strong for- ward work changed the position of affairs and in " saving " on the home line Hardman received a blow on the head which necessitated his removal to the Infirmary. Charles fortunately returned at this stage but Warrington pressed their advantage home by another try, Fish crossing easily as the result of clever passing. The Rochdale men played up splendidly and got their reward in a try near the posts which was converted. The point came from a cross- kick which Brooks safely caught, only to be robbed by Baxter before he could send, the ball dead. War- rington were now only a single point ahead and had to work hard to prevent a disaster. Fortunately the backs were too good for the Hornets and another bout of passing put the issue ibeyond doubt, Fish sending inside to Dickenson, who ran over and Preston kicked a goal.

The best man on the Warrington side was Ike Taylor, who played with rare skill and resource. Brooks stood rather too far away fiom him, and once missed a certain try for this reason. Dickenson was excellent on the defence, and saved Berry a lot of work, but he might run straighter I think whey he has the ball. The forwards were fair, but they never showed any superiority over the home pack, which contained some active and speedy men. Lees and Hockenhall were smarter even than usual, the Co-inty man doing a lot of tricky running which bothered the Hornets' defence continually, while Lees always got the ball away cleanly. Fish was the worst man on the field and was not in a fit condition for serious football. In fact if Jordan could have been secured in time the "skipper" would have had to stand down. I am glad to learn that he is in strict training this week,and hope he will set abetter example henceforth.

On the Hornets' side, Upton was probably the most prominent man, and it strikes me that he would be of more value at threequarter than full back. Baxter and Hardman were also smart and energetic. If the Hornets went in more for the passing game they would, I think, have more success. There is plenty of ir pace on the side, but it is wasted unless combination can be secured. In the second half of the game the llornets appeared to realise that kicking was a waste of time, and though a man short they were more dangerous when they changed their tactics than previously when at full strength.
Owing to Halifax's defeat by Oldham on Monday
Warrington have got among the first four, with a percentage of just 75. They ought to remain here without any very serious difficulty if the team can be kept together.

div.head: Hockey.
div.p: Hockey.

On Saturday Litchford played their return match with Eccles. Play in midfield was of an even nature but Latchford missed several chances in the circle. Half-time arrived with Eccles leading by one goal to nil. Re-starting the home team tried hard to score, but their forwards lacked judgment in shooting. Callon found the net thus equalizing, and the game ended in a draw of one goal each. For the Nisitors their full backs, Tabor and Butler played a very good game.

To-day Sefton are due at Latchford against the follow- ing team :—Goal, I. Wilkinson ; full backs,C. Hale, and T. Dixon ; half backs, D. Travis, J. B. Wilkinson and W. B. Cobb ; forwards, H. Whittle, W. Spansley, D. Knight, H. Warburton and J. Callon.

On Saturday, Stockton Heath suffered defeat at the hands of the Altrincham eleven and as the visitors had so far had a bad season,a victory for Stockton,especially after their previous week's performance,was confidently expected. For the first quarter of an hour the home side had the better of the game, and were soon leading 1-0, then a great change took place, Altrincham quickly put on 4 goals, and were leading at half-time by 4-1. In the second half, the game was very level, with Altrincham scoring one more goal to two by the home side.

Withont a doubt the better side on the day's play won, and if the Stockton Heath defence does not play better, some more defeats will have to be recorded. Of the forwards little can be said, except of course that Banks played his usual fine game and scored all three goals. •
The second eleven drew at Altrincham, and accom- plished a very smart performance, in fact they were leading five minutes from time. The final score was 14, Linnet scoring for Stockton Heath.

This week the club play Formby first and second. The first team will do well to avoid defeat, as owing to E. Pierpoint playing for Cheshire v. Lincolnshire, the back division has undergone alteration. The second eleven feel sure they can win,and I hope they will do so.

The following teams will represent Stockton Heath : First eleven (away)—R. G. Pie:point, goal ; R. Hallows and E. E. Woods, backs; A. H. Rathbone, Eric Fair- dough and J. G. Hatton (captain), halves; C. Smith, S. Baxter, W. H. Banks, %V. Richardson and A. Dolan, forwards. Referee, W.Carter. Train leaves Central 12.50. 2nd Eleven (home) : E. Fairclough, goal ; P. B. Hawtin and B. Silcock, backs ; T. Houghton, 0. M. de Jong, and H. W. Guest, halves; A. Hodgkinson, W. Linnell, C. W. Walker, L. Pierpoint, and H. Owen, for- wards. Referee, N. W. Bellamy. Bully-off, 3 o'clock. R. G. P.

Latchford 2nd visited Eccles and a fast game resulted. Eccles s,"ored twice in the first half and half-time saw them leading by 2 goals to nil. Restarting the visitors pulled themselves together and equalized, both goals coming off Banks' stick. Play had to be stopped several minutes before time owing to bad light and a drawn game resulted. To-day they journey to Sefton with the following team :—Goal, J. Appleton 1; full backs, J. Wilkinson and \V. H. Pickles ; half backs,A.N Other, G. H. Heald, and A. Shakeshaft ; forwards, J. Bruhl, W. B. Smith, E. Banks, A. Albinson, snd A Starkey.

div.head: CEMETERY HOTEL BOWLING CLUB.
div.p: THE CEMETERY HOTEL BOWLING CLUB.

On Thursday evening a large number of members and friends assembled at the Cemetery Hotel, the occasion being the presentation to Mr. J. Willett of a substan- tial chequel and gold chain for himself and wife. The members recognising the eminent services rendered to the Club for many years by Mr. Willett subscribed most generously. During the evening a telegram was read from the president of the Club, Mr.A.H. Crostield, M.P., conveying his best wishes to " his old friend Willett "and expressing his regret at being unable to be present that night. Mr. Se Taylor occupied the chair and opened the proceedings with the toast of the King, Queea, and other members of the Royal Family. This was received with musical honours. An excellent pro- gramme had been arranged, and the artistes had evidently braced themselves up specially for the occasion, as all the items were exceedingly well rendered and encores were the order. The presentation was made by the chairman who spoke in eulogistic terms of the excellent work done by their friend, Mr. Willett, for the welfare of bowling generally, in Warrington, but more especially for his own particular Club (the Cemetery Hotel Bowling Club.) He said he was inadequately expressing the feelings of his fellow members of that Club by any words of his, and the attendance there that night, and the unanimous response in the shape of subscriptions was ample evidence of the regard and esteem in which Mr. Willett was held. In handing him the chain for himself and wife he hoped the links would always remind him of the connecting links in friend- ship with the members of that Club. On rising to respond Mr. Willett was received with the singing of " For he's a jolly good fellow" and sneaking under great emotion thanked most heartily his fellow mem- bers for their beautiful presents. He would treasure them not alone for their intrinsic worth but for the kindly feeling which they expressed. Above all he I should value the token to his wife, and he hoped he might live a number of years yet to enjoy the company of his friends at the Cemetery Bowling Club. It was 12 years since he became a member of that Club and he had spent many happy hours amongst them. Other toasts were :—The Club, proposed by Mr. J. T.Whittle; The President, proposed by Mr. A. J. Jones, and responded to by Mr. J. Willett on behalf of Mr. Cros- field ; The Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Artistes. The following gentlemen contributed songs :—Messrs. J. W. Willett, .J. E. Harrison, J. Allison, Colour-Sergeant Kelly, and J. Emson. Mr. J. H. Foster carried out the duties of accompanist.
