The Aspatria Urban District Council have protested against the Postmaster-General erecting telegraph poles along their main street, as being unsightly, dangereus to traffic, and destroying the amenities of the town. "Bread is about the only thing that one cannot pawn or dispose of for beer," said Judge Smyly. K.C., at the Bow County Court on Wednesday, in giving judgment in favour of a baker against a man who said that his wife bought the goods and pawned them to buy beer.

div.head: EMMANUEL CHURCH. Aunual Sale of Work.
div.p: EMMANUEL CHURCH. Aunual Sale of Work.

Emmanuel Church and its associated institutions are the scene of great activity in religious and social work, and the past year has been one of particularly gratifying progress. The congregation is, however, faced with a heavy debt on the recently-acquired Church Institute in Knutsford-road which is fulfilling a very useful pur- pose. With the object of raising £3OO for the Institute Building Fund and Church expenses a sale of work has been held in the Institute on Wednesday, Thursday, and Friday of this week, and has been attended with success. An ardent band- of workers had thrown themselves with enthusiasm into the preparations, and the building, with its heavily-laden stalls, presented a bright and inviting appearance. The following acted as stall-holders : Minister's stall : Mrs. Vaughan and friends. Congre- gational stall : Mrs. A. Gandy and friends. Sunday school stall : Miss Booth and friends. Refreshment stall : Mr. T. Allen and friends. Household stall : Miss S. Gandy and friends. Flower and fruit stall : Mr. W. Dickens and friends. Endeavour stall : Miss S. Shepherd and friends. Tearoom: Mr. E. Allen and friends.

_ THE OPENING CEREMONY. The sale was opened on Wednesday afternoon by Mr. C. E. Parker, and the Rev. J. Manning presided over a good attendance. The Rev. F. VAUGHAN (incumbent) submitted a statement on church work. He pointed out that Emmanuel Church occupied a unique position in the Church of God and particularly in this town in which , they had been working for some years. They were glad to know that the Wesleyan Methodist Church had such a large amount of interest in and brotherly feeling towards the Reformed Episcopal Church. (Applause). It was particularly gratifying to the Emmanuel congregation to have the presence of the Rev. J. Manning and Mr. C. E. Parker. (Applause). The latter had been their friend for many years and they were proud that the president of the Free Church tonncil should open their bazaar. He (Mr. Vaughan) had been looking through the records of the church from the commencement of the movement. He found that from Easter 1893 to Novem- ber 11th of the same year the total income from church offertories was £95 6s. 3d. After they had been work- ing in the town for twenty-six years he found that the offertories for the corresponding period of 1905 amounted to £66 18s. They had, however, to consider that the first sum was collected at a time when the movement was new in the town and they had friends who were able to assist them substantially. With great gratitude he found that this year, from Easter Day to last Sunday the amount of Church offertories was .£92 2s. 21d. (Applause.) That represented a distinct advance in Sunday offertories of £25 2s. Old. over last year. (Applause.) During the same period £3O 12s. 2d. had been contributed towards the Institute and they bad supported foreign missions and other objects. Their communicants' roll numbered 146, Sunday school 260, , and men's union over 50. The Institute was purchased two years ago and upon it there remained a debt of £l6OO. During the year they had been able to pay the interest and raise £l5 towards the reduction of the debt. The Sunday school was growing so rapidly that it seemed probable that further accommodation would soon be required. (Applause). Mr. Vaughan read a list of donations to the bazaar, totalling £l7 and including £lO from Mr. Parker. The Rev. J. MANNING said the days of denomina- tional isolation were long since passed. The members of the Free Churches were no longer strangers to one another. They found it possible to help one another in various ways and to co-operate on some lines of united service that would be out of the question to isolated churches. Mr. Manning congratulated the congrega- tion of Emmanuel Church upon the part they were taking in social work. They needed, he said, to humanise their churches more and to bring them into closer touch with the lives of the people. (Applause.) The fact that Emmanuel Church had a liturgical service free from priestly pretensions and associated with a strong Evangelistic spirit filled a long-felt want in the town. Many people preferred that form of service even to the simpler services of the Nonconformist churches. He rejoiced that Mr. Vaughan had such a satisfactory report to present. (Applause). Mr. C. E. PARKER said he was much interested in the work that was being done in connection with that building and he was glad to hear the cheerful report presented by their pastor. They were certainly working in the right direction. Many Christians must be con- scious thst a great many of their Churches had got into a back water. They were ministering to a little group of people who came to them Sunday after Sunday but the great stream of life, with its good and evil and its great social problems, flowed past them uninfluenced. The Emmanuel Church workers were doing what they oould to influence the stream which passed their door. They must feel conscious of how little they could do, and the thought came tb him that the day would come when it would be possible for the Free Churches to unite where it was desirable in great missions in some central part of the town to do somewhat similar work to that which was being carried on at that Institute. (Applause.) A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Rev. J. MANNING and Mr. PARKER on the proposition of Mr. D. HODGE seconded by Mr. JOHN Ernuv. During the day musical items were given in the sale room by Miss Gandy and friends and a popular feature of the evening proceedings was the holdinr, of concerts which had been arranged by Mr. John Lloyd. Wednesday's proceeds, including donations, amounted to £64 10s. sd.

div.head: THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.
div.p: THURSDAY'S PROCEEDINGS.

Thursday's opening ceremony was pefformed by Miss B. Johnson, Stockton Heath. owing to the inclement state of the weather there was only a small attendance. The Rev. F. Vaughan presided, and said the proceeds of the first day were £1 in advance of what they were the previous year. Amongst the donations he had to announce was one of £lO from Mrs. Bibby, the proceeds of a book of household recipes which she had collected and published for the sale. Miss JOHNSON gracefully performed the ceremony allotted to her, and wished the bazaar every success. In proposing a vote of thanks to Miss Johnson, Mr. HENRY GANDY mentioned that he attended the first sale of work in connection with their Church when they raised £l6.
The vote was seconded by Mr. T. ALLEN, supported by the Rev. J. F. Ma'YTHEws and heartily accorded. _

div.head: FRIDAY'S PROCEEDINGS:
div.p: FRIDAY'S PROCEEDINGS:
THE REV. F. VAUGHAN AND "QUESTIONABLE"

METHODS OF RAISING MONEY. The sale was opened on Friday evening by the Incum- bent, (the Rev. F. Vaughan), Mr. William Atherton, church warden occupying the chair. After the devotional exercises, the chairman announced that the receipts of the two previous days amounted to £ll3 14s. lid. To this sum must be added 15s. donations. Mr. Atherton said that this gratifying result of their efforts was most encouraging and filled all hearts with gratitude. The Rev. F. VAUGHAN said that when he came to Watring.ton he found that the spirit of co-operation, sacrifice and enthusiasm of the workers of Emmanuel Church was so well known as to be almost a Lancashire proverb, and his own association with the church had proved the repucation to be well earned and equally well maintained. He was glad to know that the sums raised at Emmanuel Church for God's work were raised without the adoption of such questionable methods as raffles, draws, dances, theatrical displays, whist drives, and the like. He regretted that some churches resorted to these means. It seemed to him that whatever might be said in their favour he was per- fectly certain they could neither be classified among the fruits of the Spirit nor the additions te Faith advocated by the Apostles Peter and Paul. and how far they could be supported and carried out by Faith and Prayer, he would leave those who used them to say. He was glad that Emmanuel Church kept them- selves and their work from these dangerous pleasantries. He trusted the congregation would live to see all their hopes realised in the matter of the debt and Church extension.
Tke total proceeds of the sale amounted to .£154 10 9i

div.head: SOLDIERS' MEMORIAL. To be Unveiled by Sir Redvers Buller V.C.
div.p: THE SOLDIERS' MEMORIAL. To be Unveiled by Sir Redvers Buller V.C.

We are pleased to announce that General Sir Redvers Buller, V.C., has consented to unveil the handsome memorial to fallen soldiers which Warring- ton is erecting in Queen's Gardens. At a meeting of the Memorial Committee held at the Town Hall on Thursday, Mr. H. Roberts read a letter from Sir Redvers in answer to the Com- mittee's invitation expressing regret that it was quite impossible for him, owing to important duties which he had undertaken, to perform the ceremony before Christmas. He, however, expressed his willingness to unveil the statue if the event could be deferred until January. It was unani- mously decided to postpone the ceremony to a date convenient to Sir Redvers Buller. The decision will, we are sure, give great satisfac- tion. It is eminently fitting that General Buller should unveil the memorial as the South Lancashires, whose gallantry it will particularly commemorate, served under him in the long and arduous operations which preceded the relief Of Ladysmith, Colonel O'Leary, the respected commander 6f the regiment, it will be remembered, was killed at Pieter 's Hill during the campaign. OTICE ih HEREBY GIVEN, that the Cheshire A. County Council, at a Meeting held at Chester Castle on Thursday, the Bth day of November, 1906, made the following Bye-laws, viz. : ORGANS. No person shell in any street or public place, or on any land adjoining or near to any street or public place, use or play, or cause to be used or played, any steam organ or other musical instrument, worked by mechanical means, to the annoyance or disturbance of residents or passengers. MUSIC NEAR HOUSES. o person Shall sound or play upon any musical or noisy in,trument or sing in any street or public place within ICO yerds of nny dwelling house or office to the annoyance of any inmate thereof, after being requested to desist by such inmate, either pet :tonally or through his servant, or through a constable : krovided thnt this bye-law sha I not apply to prorerly conducted religious services, except where the request to desist is made on the ground of the serious illness of any inmate of the house. MUSIC NEAR CHURCHES. • Ho person shall so.md or play upon ',sly musical or noisy instrument or sing in any stn et or public piece within 100 yards of any piece of public worship, or public entertainment, or other place of public assembly in Which persons are for the time being assembled, to the angloyance .‘r disturbance of any person or persons co assemblea after being requested to desist by any constable or by any person so annoyed or disturbed or by zny person acting on his behalf. MUSIC NEAR HOSPITALS. No person shall sound or pla upon any musical or noisy instruno nt or sing in any street or public place within WO yards of any hospital, infirmary, convalescent home, or other place used for the recet Von or treatment of the sick after being requested to desist by any constable, or by any inmate or officer of such hospital or other place, or by any person acting on his behalf. PRNtLTIS. Any nerson who shall offend against any of the foregoing bye-laws shall be liable on summary conviction for each offence to a penalty not exceeding forty shillings. AND NOTICE IS HEREBY FURTHER GIVEN, that sealed copy of such Bye-laws hes oetn forwarded to the Secretary of State. RIGINALD POTTS, Clerk to the Cheshire County Council. Warrington Infirmary and Dispensary, The Matron begs to acknowledge, with thanks, the receipt of 20 articles of clothing from the South Lancashire Divison of the Needlework Guild. Warrington Ragged School and Mission. The limelight service on Sunday evening at the above place was conducted by Mr. E. Wynne Jones. The pictures were splendidly described, and the lessons derived from them were most interesting and instructive. The lantern was manipulated by Mr. Frank Owen with his usual ability. Bankrupt Farmer. A receiving order has been made in the County Court on the debtor's petition against Thomas Parkinson, residing and carrying on business at Brook' Farm' Orford, near Warrington, lately at Knutsford- road, Warrington, farmer. He has been adjudicated bankrupt. TABLE, FLOOR, AND HANGING LAMPS in large variety. Latest patterns.—J. S. GARLAND, Iron- monger, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. • The Nursing Association. The Hon. Treasurer of the Warrington District Nursing Association, Workingmen's Committee, begs to acknowledge with thanks the receipt of the follow- ing donations :—The Independent Order of Odd- fellows, Manchester Unity, Friendly Society, £5; The Warrington Works Bowling Association, £4 7s. 7d.; and Wm. Carson Esq., £2. Successful Local Trotting Horse. At Ashton-under-Lyne, on Monday, Mr. Tasker, of Warrington, won a mile trotting handicap of £l2 with Little Kate, beating Mr. Wild's Florizel, Stock- port, by half a length. Little Kate received 330 yards start and Florizel 240 yards. The pair afterwards met in a match for £2O which Mr. Tasker won easily by twenty lengths. Warrington Publican's Death. The death took place on Saturday of Mr. Alfred Wood, landlord of the Boar's Head Inn, Town-hill. The deceased who was 64 years of age and who leaves a widow and three sons and six daughters, was for many years in the employ of Messrs. Pearson and Knowles at their Bewsey Works, and was highly respected by both masters and fellow employees. UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS. Advt.— Burning Fatality at Warriogton. Mr. F. A. Jones, deputy coroner, held an inquest at Warrington yesterday on the body of Elizabeth Gibbons (4), daughter of Elizabeth Ann Gibbons, 14, Haydock-street, who died in the Infirmary on Tuesday from burns sustained earlier in the day. The evidence showed that the deceased and her sister went down- stairs early on Tuesday morning and that later the mother was alarmed by hearing a scream and on going to investigate, found her daughter's nightgown in flames. A verdict of " Accidental death " was returned. Cow and a Cyclist in Collision. On Monday afternoon John Connolly, butcher, of Orford-lane, was driving a cow over Warrington bridge into Bridge-street when it suddenly rushed down Mersey-street. It was stopped at the Packet Stage, and a minute later Mr. James Berry, an insurance agent, who was riding slowly down Mersey- street collided with the animal. Mr. Berry was thrown heavily to the ground, but fortunately escaped serious injury. His machine was considerably damaged owing to the cow trampling on it. N.S.P.C,C. Work. The Warrington Branch of the National Society for 'the Prevention of Cruelty to Children has during the quarter ended 30th September inquired into 62 complaints of neglect, ill-treatment and other wrongs of childhood, of which all were found to be true, affecting 201 children and 93 offenders. Action was taken as follows :-58 cases were warned, and 4 were prosecuted (convicted 4, discharged nil). The Society's Inspector made 357 visits of supervison. Golborne-street Baptist Band of Hope. Under the auspices of the above the first entertain- ment of the session was held on Tuesday when Mr. Ben Few presided over a fair audience. A capital programme was submitted, which consisted of songs, recitations and dialogues, all of which were rendered in an excellent manner by members and friends from Bank Quay, Brick-street Mission and Stockton Heath Bands of Hope. During a break in the proceedings the chairman presented certificates to three members, viz., Minnie Muir, John Muir and Edward H. Jones, who have successfully passed the examination of the Lancashire and Cheshire Band of Hope Union. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER • THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—Advt. Warrington P.S.A. There was a very good attendance at the Warring- ton P.S.A. open meeting which was held in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey-street on Sunday afternoon. Mr. Joseph Owen presided, and the speaker was the Rev. J. F. Matthews, who delivered an address on " Wanted men." Mr. Arthur Greenough sang the solo " Comfort ye " and "Waft her, angels" in a very able manner. Mr. Osborne also rendered two solos efficiently, namely, "Calvary " and " Behold I stand at the door." Mr. Walter Brough, jun., was the accompanist. Councillor Clegg read the Scripture lesson. Prayer was offered by Mr. R. Nelson. Popular Penny Concerts. There was again a crowded audience at the Bold- street Wesleyan Schoolroom on Saturday evening, when an admirable programme was given at the popular penny concert. The Rev. F. Vaughan presided Songs were given by Misses E. Barnes and May Isherwood, and Messrs. L. Aukland and R. Grounds. An action song by Elsie Whitfield and Dolly Gain, entitled" You shan't play in our yard," received an encore. Several quartettes were given in an admir- able manner byl 'Messrs. R. Grounds, J. Lloyd, L. Aukland. and H. Atkinson. Messrs. Winstanley and Paterson won much applause for several cornet solos and duets, The humourist was Mr. Alfred Grounds, who was repeatedly encored. Mr. Frank Hickman acted as accompanist. STRANGE'S A.l. Crystal LAMP OIL in barrels OT drums delivered free.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Bakers at Tea. The annual tea in connection with the Warrington Branch of the Amalgamated Union of Operative Bakers and Confectioners . was held en Saturday evening at the Lion Hotel, "about 150 sitting down to an excellent repast provided by Mr. John Lee. The after proceedings were presided over by Mr.W.H. Carr, of Leigh, chairman of the Warrington District. Loyal and other toasts were heartily drunk, a feature of the proceedings being an address by the general secretary of the Union, Mr. Jenkins. During the evening a capital musical programme was gone through. Songs were pleasingly rendered by Miss N. Carr (Leigh), and Messrs. Ditchfield (humorous), Higginbottom, F. Barnes,S. Davies and J. Howard, whilst interesting recitations were given by Mr. J. Massey and the Chairman. Mr. P. Wolfenden was the accompanist. The " Browning " Lectures. The fifth of the course of University Extension Lectures on " Robert Browning " was delivered in the Co-operative Hall on Wednesday evening by Mr. J. A. Dale, M.A. There was a good attendance. The Lecturer devoted the whole of the evening to a con- sideration of Browning's wonderful poem " The ring and the book." He said the poem was not the only one into which Browning put his most ardent spirit, but it must also rank, all things considered, 99 the greatest poetic achievement of the 19th century. It was a wonderful testimony to the passion of love which Browning bore to his fellows, to his infinite patience, and his knowledge of the smallest details of their life. If they wanted a study of human nature cut deep and done in extraordinarily full detail, lit up by all kinds of strange lights, they would not find anywhere so full and brilliant a picture as in "The ring and the book." Death of Mr. George Smith, Latchford. A well-known and highly-respected Warringtonian passed away on Tuesday in the person of Mr. George Smith, the Laurels, Latchford. The deceased, who was 53 years of age, had for many years acted in the capacity of traveller for the Firth Wire Mattress Company, Ltd., of which he was one of the founders and a director. For several years Ur. Smith's health had given Cause for anxiety to his family, but the end came suddenly after only a few days illness, and he passed away peacefully at his residence at 8.45 on Tuesday morning. His association trip]. the War- rington Rugby Club both in the capacity of a hard- working committee man and simultaneously co-trustee extended over many years, and there is no doubt that that organization owes its present ' high position in the Rugby world to his work and that of the men who were so long associated with him. An ardent worker in the friendly society movement, he did much to promote the cause of the Ancient Order of Foresters, and in his special Court (" Court Mercy" 240) he held the distinction of having passed through all the offices, and, in fact, no duty, however great or small, was too much for him.

Mr. BROOKES had promised to attend the meeting of the Council but failed to put in an appearance. In his absence the matter was explained by Councillor Stott who said that as he was about to hand over the secretaryship of the Council to Mr. Plinston he received certain information alleging that at least one member of the Board of Guardians had secured pauper labour from the workhouse at a considerably less price than was paid for ordin- ary skilled labour outside. He moved in the matter himself because he had not time to approach Mr. Plinston. He got his information from Guardians them- selves and not from the source which some members of the House Committee seemed to think. It appeared that there was a man named Clarke in the Workhouse who had a weakness for drink, but who was a very capable painter and who had done work in the Work- house. One evening a certain member of the Board went to the Workhouse and asked to see Clarke. The man was brought out, given his discharge by the master and taken to Priestly-street where he was met by a son of the member who offered him work, at sd. an hour, painting property belonging to the family. Thill rate of wages for painters was Bd. an hour and Clarke demurred at accepting sd. He was then offered 6d., and decided, that rather than be a burden to the ratepayers he would accept the pries. At the end of the week the family complained that Clarke had not done sufficient work, and he replied that he was prepared to have his work measured by a master painter to prove that he had done quite as much work as any ordinary painter would have done. Clarke gave up the job, and feeling that he could earn his living went to Manchester to purchase the necessary tools, but unfortunately spent the money on drink, and had to walk back to Warrington. Being destitute he presented himself at the \Workhouse as a new inmate. He was taken before the House Committee, when a member of the Board explained that work had been found for him but that he had refused to do it. Clarke was called an unmitigated scamp and told that he would be prose- cuted. " I seems to me," continued Councillor Stott, " that according to our poor law representatives if a man is offered 2d. an hour for painting and refuses to work on those terms he is liable to be prosecuted." Information leaked out, said , Councillor Stott, that the man had been employed at 6d. an hour and it was said that a man belonging to !another trade had been taken from the workhouse and employed by the same family at 3d. an hour less than the standard rate. He (Councillor Stott) at once called , upon the House Committee to make a full enquiry into the charge and had received the reply from Mr. Awbery which had been read by Mr. Plinston. "I deny "continued the speaker" that a thorough enquiry has been made. If it had been I should have known about it immediately but I think it has been an enquiry amongst those sympathetic to the Guardian who com- mitted the acts. We ought to protest against public representatives, sent here by the ratepayers, taking advantage of men in the workhouse. We object to members of the Board of auardians, who are supposed to represent us, employing pauper labour and displacing honest workmen who are unemployed. I hope the Council will not be satisfied but will press for a thorough enquiry into this grievance. If nothing further is done I will be prepared at our next meeting to disclose the name of the member in question." Mr. HALEY moved the resolution given above. If that sort of thing was to be allowed there was no telling where it would end. It was a distinct infringe- ment of the principles for:which we as trade unionists work. The resolution was approved. OTHER BUSINESS. FEES AT THE BEAMONT COUNCIL SCHOOL. Councillor STorr moved "That this Council protest lagainst the action of the Education Committee in deciding to make application to the Board of Education for sanction to charge school fees in the Beamont Council School and instructs the Secretary to send a copy of the resolution to the Board of Education requesting that the sanction be not granted." Counc- cillor Stott pointed out that the charging of fees would mean an income of £2BO a year—or about one-third of a penny rate. On a house rated at £3 this would mean Is. Bd. a year whereas to pay school fees, as an average would cost the parents 7s. 4d. a year. It had been understood all along that no fees were to be charged in Council schools and two prominent, officials had told him that the Board of Education would not sanction the charging of fees. Councillor Stott proceeded to explain that in the counties of Lancashire and Cheshire education was absolutely free whilst in Warrington, out ,of 13,850 scholars 5,300 attended school without paying. Mr. HALEY seconded and the resolution was approved. COUNCIL AND THE EDUCATION OF CHILDREN. At a previous meeting questions from the Committee on Industrial Education, were referred to the Executive Committee. Mr. Plinston reported that the Committee had met and drafted replies. In answer to the ques- tions they fixed the minimum age of leaving school at 13, and expressed their objection to the system of half- time attendance. Their experience as to the fitness of children on leaving the elementary schools they stated was unsatisfactory owing to the classes being too large and the curriculum overcrowded. They recommended that youths should attend technical colleges free but they did not consider that attendance at technical and evening classes snould be enforced. The action of the Committee was endorsed. Mr. POOK gave notice that Lt the next meeting he would move that the Guardians be requested to hold their rneetiggs in the evening.

COMPULSORY MILITARY TRAINING. Meeting at Warrington. • The first of a series of meetings in connection with the Warrington branch of the National Service League was held in Workingmen's Mission, Thewlis-street, on Tuesday evening. Mr. F. W. Monks presided over a fair attendance, the principal speaker being Major General Bland Strange who served in the Crimean War and Indian Mutuny and has taken a prominent part in organizing the Canadian militia. The CH/Limn/Or said he considered it a good thing that the proposals of the League had provoked so much newspaper discussion, because it enabled those who worked so hard and clisinterestly on behalf of the League to put forward its principles and proposals, and there was no doubt that by continued re-iteration a great impression would eventually be made. (Applause). Captain CROSFIELD in a short address said Lord Roberts had bald them that the day of war had not gone by, although every sensible man must wish that It had. They had, however, to face facts and it was their busi- ness to see how best they could prevent war. Lord Roberts and the League held that the best mEthod Was to be prepared for war. Lord Newton had been told by Lord Milner that if the proposals lof the League had been in force at the time of the Boer war there would have been no Boer war. The object of the League was to create a great national reserve to act as a second line of defence to guard our shores in case of any mishap to the navy or in case of the navy being scattered, and also to act as a reservoir from which we could get men to cope forward voluntarily to swell the ranks of the army if we became engaged in a big war. The League had never said and would never say that it wanted to compel men to serve outside England, as that would be unfair and unjust. What they said was that they must compel men to be trained. They believed in compulsory training and I voluntary service. (Applause). Major-General BLAND STRANGE said it was because he had seen a great deal of war that he did not want to see any more. Any man who wanted war and had seen it and who was not afraid of having it in his own country was a fool or a devil: The object of the League was to maintain peace. When nations were prepared they thought twice before they"went for" each other,but they would be very ready to go for the nation that was not prepared, especially if it was a rich nation like England. In 1806 we had a larger land force than we had at present. The population of these islands was then only. 16 millions ; now it was 42 millions. Then one man In four rendered some sort of service to the State; now it was not one man in ten. A hundred years ago we had 400,000 volunteers; now we had not half the number. Mr. Balfour had said we could not possibly be invaded,but he (the speaker) considered that a very unfortunate statement. The Major-General pointed out that the Volunteer forces rested on human enthusiasm which waxed and waned, and that was not a safe basis for the protection of the nation. The League did not advocate conscription. They only said that men should be trained so that when they wished to support the nation in a great crisis they might be worth something. (Applause.) We had a bitter lesson in South Africa, and were we going to forget it? What sort of a lesson would it be if the fighting was not in South Africa but in England? People said that with our navy invasion would be impossible. Where was the Russian navy on in to Port morning when the Japanese torpedo boats got Port Arthur ? Continuing the speaker strongly con- demned the action of the authorities in doing away with " observation " mines at our great naval and com- mercial ports. These mines were laid so that they could only be exploded when charged with a currant of electricity and were perfectly safe for our own shtpping. Was it common-sense to abolish them ? We had, continued the Major-General, been living on the memory of Nelson for 100 years. Was he going to be our national defence for another century ? The speaker strongly advocated a small professional army supplemented by the trained manhood of the nation as a second line of defence. (Applause.) On the motion of Mr. H. EINGDON seconded by Mr. GALLON and supported by "Miss BROADBENT a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to Major General Bland Strange. In moving a similar compliment to the Chairman, Captain Crosfield said the Warrington branch was making headway, the membership now being 830. (Applause.) Mr. ELWELL seconded and the motiou having been carried, the meeting concluded.
